title: Where Your Attention Should Go
script: If I handed you a list of a thousand products and asked which ones matter most, where would you start? Most people say, the expensive ones. Not quite. What matters is annual value: price times how much you sell. And when you sort a list that way, a pattern appears almost everywhere. About twenty percent of the items account for roughly eighty percent of the value. We call those A items. The next group, B, is a middle tier. And C items, often half the list, add up to just a few percent of the value. This is the idea behind ABC classification. Now, what changes? A items get close attention: frequent reviews, careful forecasts, tight control of stock, and regular talks with suppliers. C items get simple rules, like ordering a large quantity once or twice a year, because the effort of managing them is worth more than the items. I once worked with a company where planners spent most of every Monday adjusting forecasts for screws and washers. Meanwhile, the one component worth a million a year was reviewed quarterly. Nobody had decided that on purpose; it simply grew that way. The point is not the exact percentages, which vary. The point is that attention is limited, so give it where the money is. Sort first, then decide how hard to work on each group.

questions.q: What is the main idea of the lecture?
options: Cheap items deserve the most attention from every planner
Items should be ranked by value so effort goes where it counts
Suppliers should be chosen by the size of their warehouses
Every product needs exactly the same forecasting method
questions.explanation: She ends with 'give it where the money is. Sort first, then decide.'

questions.q: What share of the value do C items add up to?
options: Roughly eighty percent
About twenty percent
About half of it
Only a few percent
questions.explanation: She says C items 'add up to just a few percent of the value.'

questions.q: Why does the speaker begin by asking which products matter most?
options: To test whether students know the company's products
To show that the common answer is not quite right
To prove that expensive items are always the most important
To introduce a list she will read aloud
questions.explanation: After the question she says 'Most people say, the expensive ones. Not quite.'

questions.q: What does the speaker imply about the company she describes?
options: Its planners were right to focus on small parts
Its planners spent their time in the wrong places
Its forecasts for the costly component were excellent
Its screw supplier was unusually unreliable
questions.explanation: The costly component was reviewed only quarterly while planners worked on screws every Monday.

title: Notes That Make Things Happen
script: Have you ever left a meeting with a feeling that something important was decided, and then nothing happened? Usually the reason is in the notes. Look at this line from a real meeting summary: look into the delay with the supplier. Who is going to look into it? By when? And what does look into mean? Nobody knows, so nobody does it. A good action item has three parts: an owner, an action and a date. For example, Priya will email the supplier to confirm the new delivery date by Thursday noon. Now it's clear. One name, one verb, one deadline. Use strong verbs like send, confirm, approve or decide. Avoid soft ones such as explore or consider, because you can consider something forever. Also, don't give an action to a team. If the note says the logistics team will check stock, it means nobody will check stock, because everybody assumes a colleague will do it. Write the actions in the meeting while people are still in the room, and read them aloud at the end. That way, if someone disagrees, you hear it immediately. I like to think of vague notes as a kind of polite fiction, pleasant to read and completely useless. After the meeting, send the list within a day, and start the next meeting by reviewing it. If you make this a habit, people learn that what is said in your meetings gets done.

questions.q: What is the talk mostly about?
options: Writing clear actions with a person, a task and a date
Choosing the best software for taking notes in every kind of meeting
Making meetings shorter by removing most of the discussions
Giving teams more freedom to decide who does which tasks
questions.explanation: The speaker says a good action has an owner, an action and a date.

questions.q: Which verbs does the speaker recommend using?
options: Words such as explore and consider
Words such as discuss and hope
Words such as send, confirm and approve
Words such as look into and think about
questions.explanation: She lists send, confirm, approve and decide as strong verbs.

questions.q: Why does the speaker call vague notes 'polite fiction'?
options: To show that supplier delays are often invented by teams
To praise the writers of long and detailed summaries
To suggest they look nice but lead to no results
To explain why meeting notes should be written as stories
questions.explanation: She adds that they are pleasant to read and completely useless.

questions.q: What should a listener do after hearing the talk?
options: Give each action to the whole logistics team to be safe and fair
Wait a week before sending the meeting summary to everyone
Name a single owner for each action before the meeting ends
Use soft verbs so that people feel less pressure to deliver
questions.explanation: She says to write actions in the room with owners and read them aloud.

title: Borrowing the Past of Similar Products
script: A pharmaceutical company, a car maker and a snack brand all face the same problem: a product launches next quarter, and no sales history exists. One practical technique is forecasting by analogue. You look for similar products that launched in the past and borrow their early sales pattern. Say a company is launching a new energy drink. It might look at how its previous drink sold in the first twelve weeks, and use that shape: a slow start, a peak in month three, then a settling at a lower level. Good analogues share important traits with the new product, such as price level, target customers, distribution and promotion. But people often think any similar-looking product will do. That is a trap. A product can look alike and still sell very differently because the market has changed, because a competitor entered, or because the earlier launch was heavily advertised and this one won't be. So the best practice is to use several analogues, not one, and to show the range among them. Keep in mind the limits. Analogues tell you about shape and rough scale, not exact numbers. I'm a believer in this method, but with open eyes. It beats a blank page, and it's far better than a hopeful guess, but it's still a guess with a reason behind it. Update it as soon as real sales arrive.

questions.q: What is the main idea of the lecture?
options: Similar products' history can help forecast a launch
New products should never be forecast at all
Competitors always copy successful launches quickly
Energy drinks are the best products to launch
questions.explanation: He presents forecasting by analogue as a technique for launches with no history.

questions.q: How many analogues does the speaker recommend using?
options: None until real sales arrive
Only the most successful
More than one
Exactly one
questions.explanation: He says 'use several analogues, not one.'

questions.q: Why does the speaker mention the energy drink?
options: To recommend drinks as the best analogues
To show the right launch date for drinks
To give an example of borrowing a sales pattern
To compare drinks with cars and snacks
questions.explanation: He describes using the previous drink's first twelve weeks: 'a slow start, a peak in month three.'

questions.q: How does the speaker feel about forecasting by analogue?
options: Indifferent, because real sales always differ
Certain that it gives exact numbers
Positive, but aware of its limits
Strongly against it, since it relies on guessing
questions.explanation: He says 'I'm a believer in this method, but with open eyes.'

title: How a First Number Pulls You
script: Try this. Before you estimate how many units we will sell next month, I tell you a number: five thousand. It's a random number, from nowhere. Then I ask for your estimate. Surprisingly, your answer will probably be closer to five thousand than if I had said nothing, or said two thousand. This is anchoring: the first number we hear pulls our thinking toward it, even when we know it's random. It happens in planning all the time. Someone says last year we sold eight thousand, so let's say eight thousand again, and the whole meeting circles around that figure. Or a sales manager shouts out a target first, and everyone adjusts it slightly instead of building a view from scratch. Think about a supermarket sign that says was ten euros, now seven. The old price makes seven look like a bargain, even if the product was never worth ten. How can you protect yourself? First, make your own estimate privately before you hear anybody else's. Second, ask people to write their numbers at the same time, so nobody sets the anchor. Third, use more than one reference, for example last year, the trend and the market, and compare them. As a new planner you will often be asked for a quick number in a meeting. Take a moment to think before you answer.

questions.q: What is the main idea of the session?
options: Sales managers should never set any targets
Last year's sales are always a good guide
Random numbers are more accurate than forecasts
First numbers influence estimates, so be careful
questions.explanation: The first number pulls thinking toward it.

questions.q: What random number did the speaker use as the anchor?
options: Five thousand
Eight thousand
Two thousand
Ten thousand
questions.explanation: The speaker says 'five thousand' is the random number.

questions.q: Why does the speaker mention the supermarket sign?
options: To show how an old price flatters a new one
To explain how supermarkets choose their prices
To prove that products steadily lose value
To recommend shopping during sales periods
questions.explanation: The old price makes seven look like a bargain.

questions.q: What should a new planner do when asked for a quick number?
options: Wait for the sales manager's target
Form their own estimate before hearing others
Avoid giving numbers in meetings
Always repeat last year's figure
questions.explanation: He says to think before answering and estimate privately first.

title: Who Names the First Number
script: Who should make the first offer in a negotiation? Many people say never go first, because you'll reveal too much. But experience in many negotiations suggests the opposite when you're well prepared. The first number acts like an anchor. It pulls the whole discussion toward it. Let's say you're selling a service and you open at one hundred. The other side may counter at sixty, and you probably settle near eighty. If they had gone first at sixty, you'd likely end near seventy. So going first usually helps, as long as you know the market well. If you don't know the price range, let the other side speak first and listen carefully. Now, what if they open with an extreme offer, something absurdly low? People often think they must respond with a number of their own right away, but that is a mistake, because it treats the extreme number as a serious starting point. Instead, stay calm and ask a question. How did you reach that figure? Often the answer shows the number has no real basis. You can then bring the discussion back to facts, and make your own offer. So, in your next negotiation, prepare your range, and decide in advance whether you will speak first.

questions.q: What is the main idea of the workshop?
options: Nobody should ever make the first offer
Extreme offers should always be accepted
Services are best priced at one hundred
Opening numbers influence the outcome, so handle them deliberately
questions.explanation: The first number acts like an anchor.

questions.q: Where is the deal likely to end if the other side opens at sixty?
options: Near eighty
Near one hundred
Near sixty
Near seventy
questions.explanation: The speaker says 'you'd likely end near seventy'.

questions.q: Why does the speaker say people often feel they must answer an extreme offer at once?
options: To encourage quick counteroffers every time
To correct a mistaken idea and suggest calm
To explain how markets usually set prices
To show that extreme offers are rare
questions.explanation: She calls it a mistake and recommends asking a question.

questions.q: What should a listener do before the next negotiation?
options: Prepare a range and decide whether to open
Always let the other side speak first
Avoid negotiating when the market is unknown
Respond to every extreme offer with a number
questions.explanation: Her closing advice is to prepare the range and decide who goes first.

title: Meeting or Message
script: Before you invite eight people to a call at six a.m. for one of them, ask whether this really needs a conversation. There is a useful way to decide. A call is synchronous: everybody is present at the same moment. A written update is asynchronous: people respond when it suits them. Neither is better, and each has a price. Think about cooking. If you're making a delicate sauce, you stay by the stove and adjust it constantly, because a delay ruins it. But if you're making stew, you put it on, leave it for hours, and check occasionally. Some work is the sauce, and some is the stew. Work that is ambiguous, emotional or urgent usually needs the sauce treatment, so talk live. Routine status, requests with clear answers, and anything people need to think about before replying can be handled in writing. Across time zones, the cost of live conversation is even higher, because somebody always joins at an awkward hour. A good written update, with the context, the question and a deadline for answers, often avoids a meeting altogether. And when a thread goes beyond three exchanges without progress, that's usually the signal that people have started talking past each other. It's time to pick up the phone. Those who remember to ask this question each time will give their colleagues back something valuable: their evenings.

questions.q: What is the main point of the talk?
options: Written updates are always better than live meetings with colleagues.
Delicate sauces should be cooked by two people.
Time zones make international projects impossible.
Choose a live call or a written update depending on the work.
questions.explanation: The speaker says each has a price and compares work to a sauce or a stew.

questions.q: What does the speaker say about a thread with more than three exchanges and no progress?
options: It means that the deadline should be extended.
It proves the question has no answer.
It shows the written update was too long.
It suggests the team should switch to a call.
questions.explanation: She says that is the signal that it is time to pick up the phone.

questions.q: Why does the speaker mention cooking a sauce and a stew?
options: To show two types of work that need different levels of attention
To suggest that long meetings should always include a proper meal for everyone
To explain how to schedule calls for cooks
To show that food is cheaper in some time zones
questions.explanation: The sauce needs constant attention, the stew can be left, like live and written work.

questions.q: What does the speaker imply about unnecessary calls?
options: They are the best way to share complex data.
They are mostly caused by managers in other countries.
They take away people's personal time without good reason.
They help colleagues from different offices become friends faster.
questions.explanation: She ends by saying asking the question gives colleagues back their evenings.

title: Judging Risk by the Last Big Event
script: Let me ask you a quick question. Which is more dangerous, flying or driving? Most people say flying, but statistically, driving is far riskier per kilometre. So why do we get it wrong? Because plane crashes are dramatic. They're on every news channel for days, and they stick in our memory. This is called the availability heuristic: we judge how likely something is by how easily examples come to mind. It's a bit like judging a restaurant by the one terrible meal you had there, and forgetting the twenty good ones. Now, in a company, this shows up all the time. Suppose a supplier delivered late once, and it caused a very stressful week. From then on, everyone remembers that supplier as unreliable, even if the data shows ninety-five percent on-time delivery. Meanwhile, a quieter supplier with a slow, steady decline gets ignored, because nobody has a memorable story about it. I find this a little worrying, honestly, because it means our attention goes to the loudest problem, not the biggest one. The fix is to ask for the numbers before you decide. How often does it happen, and how bad is it, on average? Stories are useful for understanding, but they're terrible for measuring. Keep that in mind when you write your reports.

options: We often judge risk by how easily examples come to mind.
News channels should stop reporting on accidents altogether.
Flying is safer than driving in every country of the world.
Suppliers should be replaced immediately after any single late delivery.
questions.explanation: The speaker defines the heuristic as judging likelihood by how easily examples come to mind.

questions.q: What was the on-time delivery rate of the supplier that delivered late once?
options: Fifty percent
Ninety-five percent
One hundred percent
Twenty percent
questions.explanation: She says the data shows ninety-five percent on-time delivery.

questions.q: Why does the speaker mention the restaurant?
options: To show that restaurants carry more risk than airlines do
To compare the idea to something familiar from daily life
To suggest where the students should have lunch after the class

questions.explanation: It is an analogy: judging a place by one bad meal and forgetting twenty good ones.

options: She is amused by how rarely it happens.
She finds it somewhat concerning.

She thinks it is a clever way to save time.
questions.explanation: She says she finds it worrying because attention skips the biggest problem.

title: Same Shortage, Different Experience
script: Two customers order the same product on the same day, and we don't have it. Customer one hears, we'll ship it as soon as it's back in stock. Customer two hears, sorry, we can't supply that. Same shortage, very different outcomes. The first situation is a backorder: the order is kept, and it will be filled later. The second is a stockout in the strict sense: the sale is lost, or the customer simply goes elsewhere. Which of the two do you think costs more? It depends. A backorder keeps the revenue, but it brings extra work: tracking the order, shipping in pieces, sometimes paying for express transport to catch up. And the customer waits, which hurts trust. A lost sale costs the margin right away, and may cost the customer for good. In a market where buyers can switch easily, say consumer electronics, a stockout is usually the worse one. In a market with few suppliers, like a specialized industrial part, customers will often accept a backorder. So before you decide how much stock to hold, ask which one your customers will tolerate. And tell your colleagues in sales and customer service, because they need to say the right thing on the phone. The shortage is the same. What the customer lives through is not.

questions.q: What is the main idea of the talk?
options: Backorders are always cheaper than stockouts
Customers should never be told about shortages
Sales teams should decide how much stock to hold
A shortage costs different amounts by handling
questions.explanation: She compares the two outcomes and says 'The shortage is the same. What the customer lives through is not.'

questions.q: What extra cost may a backorder bring?
options: Losing the profit on the sale immediately
Paying for express transport to catch up
Lowering the price for all customers
Hiring new sales staff
questions.explanation: She lists 'sometimes paying for express transport to catch up.'

questions.q: Why does the speaker ask which of the two costs more?
options: To argue that stockouts are always worse
To criticize customers who switch suppliers easily
To make the audience think before she answers
To show she already knows the exact answer
questions.explanation: Her answer is 'It depends,' followed by examples from two markets.

questions.q: What should a planner do before setting stock levels?
options: Promise a backorder to every single customer
Find out which shortage customers will accept
Treat every shortage as a lost sale
Hold the same stock level in all markets
questions.explanation: She says 'ask which one your customers will tolerate.'

title: Small Batches and Short Waits
script: Let's do a little experiment in our heads. You and two colleagues must prepare one hundred letters. Each letter needs three steps: fold, put it in an envelope, and seal. Each step takes ten seconds per letter. Option one: do it in one big batch. Person one folds all one hundred letters, which takes a thousand seconds. Only then does person two start stuffing, and then person three seals. The first finished letter appears after about two thousand and ten seconds, more than thirty minutes, and the whole job takes fifty minutes. Option two: pass the letters on in batches of ten. Person one folds ten, which takes a hundred seconds, and passes them on right away. Now all three work in parallel. The first batch of ten is finished after three hundred seconds, and the whole job takes about twenty minutes. Same people, same speed, much shorter waiting. It's the same reason a supermarket cashier doesn't wait until your whole trolley is full before scanning the first item. Nothing was sped up. The only thing we changed was how much waited at each step. Big batches look efficient, because each person stays busy, but they make everything else wait. So if a customer is asking why an order is late, look at the batch sizes. Smaller batches nearly always shorten the wait.

options: Three people always work faster than two
Smaller batches cut waiting time at the same speed
Faster workers are the best way to finish jobs
Folding is the slowest of the three steps
questions.explanation: Same people, same speed, much shorter waiting.

questions.q: How long does the whole job take in batches of ten?
options: About twenty minutes
About thirty minutes
About twelve minutes
About fifty minutes
questions.explanation: The speaker says the whole job takes about twenty minutes.

questions.q: Why does the speaker mention the supermarket cashier?
options: To show that cashiers work faster than office staff do
To explain exactly how letters should be folded
To give a familiar case of not waiting for a full batch
To suggest that supermarket trolleys should be smaller
questions.explanation: The cashier scans the first item without waiting for the full trolley.

options: Hire more people for each step

questions.explanation: The speaker says to look at the batch sizes.

title: Looking at the System, Not the Person
script: A shipment goes to the wrong warehouse. The first question in many companies is, who did this? Does that question ever make anything better? In my experience, it makes people hide mistakes, and hidden mistakes come back. A blameless review does the opposite. After something goes wrong, you ask how the system allowed it, not who failed. Take our wrong warehouse example. The person who typed the address made an error, yes. Ask why it was possible to type a free text address. Ask why there was no check against the customer record. Ask why she was working alone, at the end of a twelve-hour day. When you ask these questions, you find causes that can be fixed. If you only blame the person, the same mistake will be made by the next person, because the system hasn't changed. Blameless does not mean without responsibility. People still own their actions, and they still need to learn. It means separating learning from punishment. In the review, write a timeline of what happened, what each person knew at the time, and which changes would prevent it next time. As team leads, how you react in the first five minutes decides everything. If people see you stay calm and curious, they'll tell you the truth next time, and the truth is the only thing that makes the system stronger.

options: Free text addresses should be allowed in all kinds of shipping systems.
After errors, look at the process rather than for someone to blame.
Reviews should be done only when a customer complains very loudly.

questions.explanation: The speaker says to ask how the system allowed the error, not who failed.

questions.q: What does the speaker say a review should include?
options: A timeline, what people knew, and ways to stop a repeat
A report to the customer about the money that was lost
A list of the staff who should receive extra training soon

questions.explanation: He lists a timeline, what each person knew, and changes to prevent it.

options: To make the audience think about whether blame is helpful
To find out which person in the audience made the error

Stay calm and curious so that people speak openly

questions.explanation: He says calm, curious leaders get the truth, which strengthens the system.

title: A Small Flick, A Big Crack
script: Picture a supermarket that sells ten jars of pasta sauce a week. One week it sells twelve. The store manager thinks, better order extra, so she orders twenty. The distributor sees twenty and decides demand is rising, so he orders fifty from the factory. The factory sees fifty and builds a hundred. Nothing real happened except two extra jars, yet the factory is now planning for a boom. This is called the bullwhip effect: a small flick of the wrist at the handle becomes a violent crack at the tip. Each step adds a little safety margin, and the margins multiply. I find it almost funny how reasonable every single decision is, and how unreasonable the final result looks. By the way, I once tried a real bullwhip at a festival and nearly hit myself in the face. Anyway, back to the point. So what can we do? Two fixes work well in practice. First, share real sales data upstream, so the factory sees the ten and the twelve, not the fifty. Second, shorten the delays and the order batches, because big, rare orders exaggerate every wobble. Let's say the store orders every day instead of once a month. The swings shrink at once. Frankly, I think the first fix is the cheaper one, and companies ignore it far too often. The take-away: stop reacting to orders, and start looking at what customers actually buy.

options: Factories should hold large stocks of finished goods at all times
Supermarkets forecast their sales better than distributors do
Small demand changes get amplified as they move up the chain
Order sizes should be as large and as rare as possible
questions.explanation: The pasta sauce example shows twelve jars becoming a factory order of a hundred.

questions.q: According to the speaker, what happens if a store orders every day instead of once a month?
options: Demand rises sharply at the factory level
Nothing changes in the supply chain at all
The swings become even more extreme overall
The swings get smaller straight away
questions.explanation: He says that if the store orders every day, 'the swings shrink at once.'

questions.q: Why does the speaker mention using a real bullwhip at a festival?
options: To prove he understands how factories plan production
To show that the effect can be dangerous for workers
To make a brief personal remark before moving on
To give a second example of demand being amplified
questions.explanation: He follows the story with 'Anyway, back to the point,' which closes the digression.

options: It is the cheaper fix and companies underuse it
It is a costly step that most firms already do well
It is a risky idea that few companies should try
It is a minor fix compared with changing the factory plan
questions.explanation: He says the first fix 'is the cheaper one, and companies ignore it far too often.'

title: One Slow Step Sets the Pace
script: Picture a kitchen with five stations: chopping, grilling, plating, packing, and delivery. Grilling can handle sixty meals an hour, but the oven for the final finish handles only forty. How many meals leave the kitchen per hour? Forty, whatever the other stations do. The slowest step sets the pace for the whole system, and that step is the bottleneck. The same applies to a plant. It may have fast filling lines, spacious warehouses and a generous packing area, yet if one mixing tank or one inspection machine is slower than the rest, that is the limit on output. The consequence is counterintuitive. If you add capacity at a step that isn't the bottleneck, nothing improves. The extra product simply queues in front of the slow step, and inventory rises. Meanwhile, every minute lost at the bottleneck is a minute lost for the entire plant, so protecting its time becomes critical: keeping it supplied, avoiding changeovers, and scheduling maintenance when it is not needed. Where does that leave the planner? You schedule around the constraint. Orders are released at the rate the bottleneck can process, not at the rate the sales team hopes for. And be aware that, once you relieve one bottleneck, another step becomes the new limit. Improvement is therefore a cycle of finding the constraint, relieving it and looking again.

questions.q: What is the main idea of the talk?
options: Warehouses are the usual cause of delays
Sales teams should set the pace of production
One slow step limits the whole plant's output
Every station should have the same equipment
questions.explanation: She says 'The slowest step sets the pace for the whole system.'

questions.q: How many meals per hour leave the kitchen in the example?
options: Forty meals
Sixty meals
Twenty meals
One hundred meals
questions.explanation: She answers her own question: 'Forty, whatever the other stations do.'

questions.q: Why does the speaker say that another step becomes the new limit?
options: To argue that planners are usually wrong
To explain why kitchens often fail
To show that improvement is an ongoing cycle
To warn planners against fixing any bottlenecks
questions.explanation: She concludes 'Improvement is therefore a cycle of finding the constraint, relieving it and looking again.'

questions.q: What does the speaker imply about buying a faster filling line when a mixing tank is the constraint?
options: It will not raise the plant's total output
The mixing tank will become faster too
Inventory in the plant will fall

questions.explanation: She says adding capacity at a non-bottleneck step means 'nothing improves.'

title: Why Change Projects Fail
script: A company spends a year and a lot of money on a new planning system. The software works perfectly. Six months after launch, half the team is still using their old spreadsheets. The reason is that change projects rarely fail on technology. They fail on people. Let's look at three reasons, and then at what to do about them. The first is a lack of understanding. If staff hear about a change only when it arrives, they fill the silence with rumours. They imagine the worst, usually job losses. The second is the cost to the individual. A new tool means a temporary drop in competence. Someone who was the expert is now a beginner. Naturally, that person resists, even though the organisation benefits. The third is a lack of reinforcement. Without managers who use the new system themselves and ask for its outputs in meetings, the old habits win quietly. Does any of this sound like a project you know? Probably. The remedy is not a better announcement. It's involving people early, giving them time to practise safely, and making sure the new way is the easiest way. After this overview, we'll examine each of these three causes through a short case. For now, remember this: you can install a system in a weekend, but adopting it takes months, and it's the second part that decides success.

options: New planning software is rarely worth the money it costs a company.
Staff should be told about changes only on the day of launch.
Change projects fail mostly because of people, not technology.
Old spreadsheets are better than any modern planning system.
questions.explanation: The speaker says change projects rarely fail on technology; they fail on people.

questions.q: How many reasons for failure does the speaker give?
options: Two main reasons
Six main reasons

questions.explanation: The speaker says there are three reasons.

options: To invite the students to criticise the speaker's examples

questions.explanation: The question links the three causes to familiar projects, and the speaker adds 'Probably'.

options: Look at each of the three causes using a short case

questions.explanation: The speaker says they will examine each cause through a short case.

title: When More Choices Make Things Worse
script: I once worked with a team that had to pick a new tool for tracking shipments. They compared twenty-three options. Twenty-three! Every week they added a new column to their comparison sheet. After four months, they still hadn't chosen anything, and the old system was getting worse. That's choice overload. When there are too many options, people don't make better decisions. They make slower ones, or they don't decide at all. And if they do choose, they often feel less happy, because they keep thinking about the options they gave up. Think about a restaurant menu with ten pages. You spend twenty minutes reading, you order the same pasta as always, and you still wonder if the fish was better. So what can a team lead do? First, set the criteria before you look at the options. Second, cut the list to three. Not ten, not five. Three. Third, set a deadline for the decision, and say clearly that a good choice today is better than a perfect choice in June. Of course, you might lose the perfect option this way. But a perfect option that never gets chosen isn't worth much. The lesson is simple: when you give people everything to choose from, you may be giving them nothing.

options: Thirty-three options

questions.explanation: The speaker says the team compared twenty-three options.

title: Checking You Understood
script: On a call, there's a moment every non-native speaker knows. Someone speaks quickly, you catch about eighty percent, and you decide to stay quiet. Later you realise you missed the main point. I once worked with a planner who did exactly that. She nodded for a whole meeting, then sent the wrong order quantity because she had misheard a number. The good news is that a clarifying question doesn't make you look unprepared. It makes you look careful. The trick is how you ask. One way is to repeat back what you heard: So, just to confirm, you need two thousand units by the twelfth, is that right? This shows you were listening, and it lets the other person correct you. Another way is to ask about one specific part. Could you say that last number again? Or, when you say next week, do you mean Monday or Friday? Avoid questions like, sorry, I didn't understand anything. That sounds like you weren't paying attention. Be specific, and be early. Ask while the topic is still being discussed, not after the call has moved on. If you can't ask during the call, send a short message right afterwards. So the next time you have a doubt, remember this: a thirty-second question is much cheaper than a wrong shipment.

Learning new vocabulary before a long conference call

questions.explanation: The speaker says she misheard a number and sent the wrong order quantity.

title: Keeping Goods Cold All the Way
script: Vaccines, insulin, some foods: they all share one problem. They only stay good inside a temperature range, often between two and eight degrees. The cold chain is the series of steps that keeps them there, from the factory, through warehouses and trucks and airports, all the way to the customer's fridge. And the key word is chain. It only needs to fail once. A pallet can sit on a hot airport apron for forty minutes, and nobody notices, until the data logger tells a different story. Where does it usually break? In my experience, not in the freezers themselves. Those are monitored and alarmed. It breaks in the handovers: the dock between a truck and a warehouse, the customs shed, the last mile to the pharmacy. These are the places where nobody feels fully responsible. The good news is that you can design for it. You can use insulated packaging with a known protection time, place loggers in every shipment, and agree in advance on what happens if a reading goes out of range. Product that has left the range, even briefly, may have to be quarantined and tested. That costs far more than the fuel for a refrigerated truck. Warehouse staff sometimes say the cold chain is the only chain that gets weaker when it's warm. Quite. So treat every handover as a risk, not as a formality.

options: How to build a freezer for a large warehouse
Why vaccines are more expensive than other products
How sensitive goods are protected and where that fails
Which airports have the best loading docks
questions.explanation: He defines the cold chain and then explains where it 'usually breaks.'

questions.explanation: He says it 'may have to be quarantined and tested.'

title: Hunting for Evidence We Already Like
script: Here's a pattern I've seen in nearly every planning review. Someone believes demand for a product is about to grow. They open the data, and, what a coincidence, they find three charts that agree. That's confirmation bias: we search for, notice and remember the information that supports what we already think. It rarely feels like bias from the inside. It feels like diligence. Let's take a regional sales lead who is convinced a new distributor is performing brilliantly. She filters the report to the two months when orders spiked, and she never scrolls to the quarter when returns doubled. Nothing she presented was false. It was simply incomplete, and incompleteness is far harder to challenge than error. Of course, I'm told that analysts are entirely objective creatures, so I'm sure none of us has ever done this. The remedy isn't more willpower. It's structure. Before you look at the data, write down what result would change your mind. Ask a colleague to argue the opposite case, and give them time to prepare it properly. And when a number confirms your hunch very neatly, treat that as a reason to check it twice, not a reason to stop. As team leads, you set the standard here. If you reward the tidy story, you'll keep getting tidy stories, and the awkward facts will quietly stay out of the room.

options: Analysts should avoid using filtered reports in any situation.
Distributors perform better when managers review the data weekly.

questions.explanation: The speaker defines the bias and says the remedy is structure.

questions.q: What happened in the quarter that the sales lead did not show?
options: Returns doubled
Orders spiked
The distributor changed its prices
Demand stopped growing
questions.explanation: She never scrolls to 'the quarter when returns doubled'.

questions.q: Why does the speaker say analysts are 'entirely objective creatures'?

To gently mock the idea that anyone is immune to this bias

title: Three Numbers, One Plan
script: Ask sales, finance and operations for next quarter's number, and you'll get three different answers, each defendable. Sales gives the number they hope to win, usually the highest. Finance gives the number in the budget, which is often a target set months ago. Operations gives the number they can realistically produce and ship, which depends on capacity and supply. None of them is lying. They answer different questions. So a consensus forecast is not a compromise in the sense of averaging three numbers. It's a process. First, start from one shared baseline, usually a statistical forecast. Second, each function adds what it knows. Sales brings customer news. Finance brings pricing and budget limits. Operations brings constraints. Third, differences are discussed in a meeting, and every adjustment needs a reason that can be written down. Fourth, a leader decides, and the agreed number becomes the single plan everyone works to. It's said that a camel is a horse designed by a committee. A consensus forecast is the effort to avoid that, which is why the rules matter. Importantly, the target and the forecast may stay different numbers; the gap between them is a problem to discuss, not to hide. Let's look at the first of those steps in more detail, because most meetings go wrong right at the start.

options: Finance numbers are always the most accurate
Sales should decide the final forecast alone
Departments differ and need a process to agree
Meetings should be avoided in forecasting
questions.explanation: He says 'None of them is lying. They answer different questions,' then describes a process.

options: The statistical baseline
The limit of production capacity
The highest customer estimate
The number set in the budget
questions.explanation: He says 'Finance gives the number in the budget.'

options: To joke that group decisions can go wrong
To explain how animals are used in transport

questions.explanation: He adds 'which is why the rules matter.'

title: What to Check in a Supply Contract
script: Contracts are written by lawyers, but they're used by planners, and I think that's a problem. So let me go through four clauses that affect your daily work. First, volumes. Does the contract promise a minimum quantity that you must buy, or a maximum the supplier will provide? If you forecast ten thousand units and the cap is eight thousand, you'll find out the hard way. Second, lead times. Look for the stated time between order and delivery, and for how it's measured. From order date or from confirmation? A difference of three days can matter a lot. Third, penalties. What happens if the supplier is late, or if you cancel? Some contracts charge a fixed amount per day, others a percentage of the order value. Know which one you have, and who can apply it. Fourth, force majeure. This clause covers events outside anyone's control, such as floods or a port closing. It decides who bears the cost when those occur. I'm told contracts are meant to be read before signing, which is the sort of rumour I'd like to see confirmed. Naturally, you don't have to be a lawyer. Highlight these four clauses, summarise them on one page, and share it with the team. Then, when something goes wrong, you'll know your rights in minutes, not days.

options: Four contract clauses that planners should understand
Ways to avoid signing supply contracts in the future
How lawyers draft long agreements for large suppliers
The causes of floods and port closings around the world
questions.explanation: The speaker goes through volumes, lead times, penalties and force majeure.

options: Whether the supplier can raise its prices during the year
How the lead time is calculated from the order date
How many units the buyer must order each month

questions.explanation: The speaker says it decides who bears the cost of such events.

title: Is This Change Real or Just Noise
script: I once worked with a planner who panicked every time weekly sales moved by ten percent. She'd call a meeting, change the forecast and, a week later, the numbers would bounce back. She was reacting to noise. Every process has natural variation. If you measure orders every week, you'll never get exactly the same number twice. The question is whether a new number is just part of that normal wobble, or a real signal that something has changed. A control chart helps you decide. You plot your numbers over time, work out the average, and draw two lines, one above and one below, that mark the normal range. A common rule is to set them roughly three standard deviations away, but you don't need the maths to get the idea. If a point sits inside the lines, treat it as noise and do nothing. If a point lands outside, or if you see seven points in a row on the same side of the average, something has probably changed, and it's worth investigating. Let's say weekly returns usually sit between forty and sixty. A week with fifty-five is fine. A week with ninety is a signal. The benefit is calm. You stop overreacting to ordinary swings, and you stop missing the swings that matter. Before you change anything next time, ask yourself whether the number is even outside the normal range.

options: Telling normal variation from a real change in a process

questions.explanation: The speaker explains how a control chart separates noise from a signal.

options: Forty points

Ninety points

questions.explanation: The speaker says seven points in a row on the same side suggests a change.

title: Putting a Number on Waiting
script: When a project is late, we usually say it's a shame. But how much of a shame? Cost of delay answers that question with a number: how much value do we lose for each week the project is not finished? Imagine two projects and only one team. Project A would save eight thousand euros a month. Project B would bring in two thousand a month. If A takes four months and B takes one, which comes first? Many people say B, because it's quick. Let's check. If we do B first, A starts after one month, so we delay A's savings by one month and lose eight thousand. If we do A first, B waits four months, and we lose four times two thousand, so eight thousand as well. It's a tie. Now suppose B takes two months. Doing B first would delay A by two months, so the loss doubles to sixteen thousand, and suddenly A is the better start. The rule of thumb is to divide the monthly value by the duration, and do the highest number first. I should mention that I once learned this in a very long course. Anyway, back to the point. The point is that without a number, the loudest person tends to set the order. With a number, you can have a calmer argument. The numbers will be rough, but even a rough number beats a feeling.

options: Finishing every single project as quickly as the team possibly can
Hiring more teams to run several projects together

questions.explanation: The speaker explains cost of delay as value lost for each week.

options: Four thousand euros a month

title: The Same Sentence, Different Meaning
script: Take a simple sentence: that will be difficult. In some business cultures, it means exactly what it says, and the discussion goes on. In others, it is the polite way of saying no, and a foreign negotiator who keeps pushing seems to be missing the point. This is the first of the differences I want to discuss: directness. Some cultures value saying things explicitly, and some value protecting the other person's face, so a refusal arrives wrapped in suggestions and softeners. Second, hierarchy. In some organizations the person at the table can agree to a deal. In others, the real decision-maker is not in the room, and the meeting is for building relationship and gathering information. Pushing for a signature there can backfire. Third, time. Is a deadline a promise or a target? Is arriving ten minutes late disrespectful or normal? Incidentally, I once spent a week in a country whose bus timetable I never fully understood, but that's beside the point. Back to our topic. These patterns are tendencies, not rules, and every person is an individual, so use them to ask better questions, not to build stereotypes. Before an international negotiation, find out who decides, how directly people speak and how they view time. And when something puzzles you, check your reading instead of assuming. A short clarifying question is cheap, and a wrong assumption can be very expensive.

options: The same words can carry different meanings across business cultures
International meetings should avoid talking about deadlines
Directness is always the best approach in negotiations
Every country has a fixed set of negotiating rules
questions.explanation: The speaker covers directness, hierarchy and time.

questions.q: What might 'that will be difficult' mean in some cultures?
options: A polite way of refusing
A request for a lower price
A statement about delivery timing
An invitation to keep pushing
questions.explanation: He says it can be the polite way of saying no.

questions.q: Why does the speaker mention the bus timetable?
options: To illustrate the idea of hierarchy

To show that public transport is better abroad
questions.explanation: He says it is beside the point and returns to the topic.

title: Why Shipments Get Stuck
script: Why does a shipment that looked perfectly on time on Thursday suddenly show no movement for six days? Very often, the answer is customs. Let's walk through the usual causes. The first is paperwork. A missing invoice, a wrong weight, or a company name spelled differently on two documents can stop everything. The second is classification. Every product has a code that decides the duty and the rules that apply. If the code is wrong, or if the officer reads the description differently, the goods wait while the question is sorted out. The third is inspection. Some boxes are chosen for checks at random, and others because the product is sensitive. You don't control that. What you can control is how much room you leave. Experienced planners add a buffer to the lead time for every border crossing, based on the history of that route, not a guess. They also keep their documents consistent and check them before the truck leaves, not after it arrives. And they talk to their forwarder early, since a good one often spots a problem before the authorities do. Notice that none of this makes customs faster. It simply makes your plan stronger when customs is slow, which, if we're honest, is more often than we would like.

title: How Bad Data Quietly Bends a Report
script: Let's start with a simple dashboard that shows average order value. It says three hundred euros. The sales team is pleased. But nobody checks what's behind that number. Suppose ten percent of orders were entered twice. Now the system counts the same big orders two times, and the average goes up. Or suppose some orders are missing because an integration failed on Tuesday night. If the missing ones are the small orders, the average climbs again. In both cases, the report looks fine. There's no error message, no red warning, just a number that's quietly wrong. That's why data quality problems are dangerous: they don't fail loudly. I once spent an afternoon reading about how dashboards are designed in my favourite colour scheme, but, well, anyway, back to the point. There are two main types of problem. Missing records make your totals too low, or hide a pattern. Duplicated records inflate totals and give extra weight to some customers. Both distort the story. What can you do? First, compare totals against another source, such as the finance system. Second, count records at each step and look for sudden changes. Third, ask what is not in the report. We'll turn to those checks in more detail after the break, with a short exercise on a real data set.

questions.explanation: The speaker says data problems don't fail loudly and quietly distort reports.

options: It goes up.
It goes down.
It stays the same.
It shows an error message.
questions.explanation: He says that if missing orders are small, the average climbs.

title: Turning Stock Into Time
script: Suppose I tell you we have forty thousand units of a product in the warehouse. Is that a lot? A little? Honestly, you can't say, and neither can I, because a quantity means nothing without a rate. That's the whole motivation for days of supply. You take the stock and divide it by the average daily demand, and the answer is expressed in time. Forty thousand units, selling two thousand a day, gives twenty days. Suddenly, a finance colleague, a manager or a customer service lead understands the situation without knowing anything about units, packs or pallets. They hear twenty days, and they can compare it with how long a resupply takes. If the next delivery needs thirty days, you have a problem that can be explained in one sentence. Incidentally, I once spent a whole flight trying to remember why one country calls a store a depot while another says warehouse. It doesn't matter. Back to the point. Notice, though, that days of supply is only as honest as the demand figure behind it. If a promotion has inflated recent sales, your cover will look shorter than it really is. And if demand is about to fall, it will look reassuring when it shouldn't. So treat it as a translation device, a way to make a stock number speak a language that everyone shares, and always ask what demand assumption sits underneath.

questions.q: How many days of supply are there in the example?
options: Thirty days

options: To give an example of calculating cover

title: Scoring Options Fairly
script: You have four possible suppliers, and every colleague has a favourite. How do you make a choice without it turning into a contest of opinions? A weighted decision matrix can help. Step one: agree on the criteria before you look at the options. Say price, delivery reliability, quality and support. Step two: give each criterion a weight, from one to five, based on what matters most. Reliability might get five, support only two. Step three: score each supplier on each criterion, from one to ten. Then multiply score by weight, add up the totals and compare. The result is a table that everyone can read. The real benefit is the conversation. Instead of arguing about who is best, people discuss what matters and why. However, be clear about what a matrix does not prove. It does not give you the truth; it organises your judgement. If you change the weights slightly, the winner may change, so test that. And if the result surprises you, don't hide it. Ask why. Maybe the matrix is missing a criterion, or maybe your instinct was biased. I always say that a spreadsheet makes any opinion look like a fact, which is a skill worth being careful with. Use the matrix to support the discussion, not to replace it.

options: A matrix gives structure to a choice but not the truth.

questions.explanation: The speaker says the matrix organises judgement and does not give the truth.

options: Hide the table and rely on instinct

title: Why We Keep the Pre-Selected Choice
script: Here's a curious fact about human behavior: when a choice is already made for us, we usually keep it. If a form comes with a box ticked, most people leave it ticked. If a retirement plan enrolls you automatically, most stay in, and if it requires you to sign up, a far smaller share does. That's the default effect, and it works for several reasons. Changing the option takes effort, however small. The default also looks like a recommendation, a sign of what most people choose or what the experts prefer. And moving away from it feels like taking a risk, because if things go badly you chose the change. I'm reminded of the first time I tried to cancel a streaming subscription, which took eleven clicks, but that's another topic. Back to the point. Designers know all this. A well-built system for ordering supplies can set the default quantity to the standard pack, the default carrier to the approved one, and the default date to the next planned delivery. Used well, defaults guide people toward good decisions without taking choice away. Used badly, they trap people into costs they never noticed. Personally, I think anyone who designs a form or a system has a responsibility here, because the default is the most powerful choice on the screen. When you set one, ask whose interest it serves.

title: One Supplier or Two
script: Imagine your factory buys one key ingredient from one supplier. Life is simple. One contract, one contact person, one price. And honestly, a single supplier can give you a better price, because you buy more from them. You also build a close relationship, so they might help you in an emergency. But what happens if that supplier has a fire, or a strike, or just a bad month? Your whole line can stop. That's the risk of single sourcing. Dual sourcing means two suppliers for the same item. You pay a bit more per unit, and you need to manage two relationships. But if one fails, the other can step in. Now, people often think dual sourcing means splitting the order fifty-fifty. But that's not necessary. Many companies buy eighty percent from the main supplier and twenty from the second. The small share keeps the second supplier ready, with the paperwork done and the product approved. Let's say the main one stops for a month. The second can grow its volume. It won't be instant, but it's far faster than finding a new one from zero. So, as a planner, your job is not to remove all risk. It is to ask: what would it cost us if this supplier stopped, and is a second source cheaper than that?

title: Ending Meetings on Time
script: A meeting that ends on time doesn't happen by luck. It's built before anyone joins the call. People often think the agenda is the most important part. But an agenda is only a list of topics. What you really need is a purpose. Ask yourself one question: what will be different when this meeting is over? If the answer is we'll all be updated, send an email instead. Next, give every decision an owner. Let's say you're discussing a delayed shipment of packaging material. The question is not should we worry about it. The question is who will decide whether to pay for air freight, and by when. Put that name next to that item. When the owner is clear, discussion gets shorter, because someone is responsible for closing it. Then, keep an eye on the clock. If an item runs over, don't let it eat the whole hour. Park it, name who will follow up, and move on. Finally, close properly. In the last three minutes, read back the decisions and the actions, with names and dates. Nobody likes this part, and that's exactly why it works. Notice that none of this takes extra time. It simply moves the thinking to the start and the end. The people who skip those two moments are the ones who schedule a second meeting to repeat the first.

title: Staying Calm When Someone Is Angry
script: Sooner or later, the person across the table gets angry. Maybe a delivery was missed, or a price was rejected, and suddenly the voice is raised. Your instinct will be to defend yourself or to raise your own voice. Resist it. Anger is information, and your job is to stay steady long enough to read it. First, breathe, and slow your speech down. A calm voice is surprisingly contagious. Second, let the person finish. Interrupting an angry person is like blowing on a fire. Third, name the feeling, gently. You can say: I can see this delay has caused real problems for you. You're not agreeing that you're wrong, only that the emotion is real. Often the temperature drops within seconds, because people calm down when they feel heard. By the way, I once tried to practice this with my teenage nephew over a video game, and I lost both the argument and the console. Anyway, back to the point. After the feeling has been named, move to problem solving: what do you need, and what can we do by Friday? Only then does the substance of the negotiation come back. We have now covered how to respond in the moment. The next section turns to the opposite situation: what to do when you notice that you yourself are getting angry.

title: Seeing the Whole Chain
script: A factory can be proud of its numbers: record output, low costs, almost no downtime. And still, the customer waits. How is that possible? Because a chain is not measured at its best link. I once worked with a plant that had pushed its packaging line to maximum speed. Everyone cheered. But the labeling area downstream was slower, so pallets piled up in the corridor, and the delivery date for customers did not improve at all. We had optimized one link and made the whole chain a bit worse, since the extra work in progress was now in the way. End-to-end visibility means seeing the whole journey: raw materials arriving, production, quality checks, warehouse, transport, and the customer's receipt. When you see all of it, you notice where goods wait, rather than where they are busy. Most of the time in any chain is waiting, not working. And that is where the delay hides. In practical terms, this is about shared data and shared goals. If the production team is judged by output, and the logistics team is judged by cost, they'll make decisions that look right locally and wrong overall. So when you ask for a report, ask what it connects to. A number that sits alone can be quite misleading.

options: Raw materials

title: Why We Overvalue What We Own
script: Picture a simple negotiation. You own an old server rack that has been sitting in storage for three years. A colleague offers you five hundred euros for it. You say no. A week later, a different department is selling an identical rack, and you wouldn't pay more than three hundred. Same object, same condition. Yet your price changed. That's the endowment effect: once something is ours, we value it more than we would if we didn't own it. We don't just see the object, we see our history with it, and we feel that giving it up is a loss. In negotiations this causes real friction. Sellers anchor on what the thing means to them, while buyers anchor on what it would cost to replace. Both sides feel they're being reasonable, and the gap between them looks like an insult. Why does this matter for you? Because it works inside companies too, with budgets, territories and long-running projects that everyone is reluctant to close. So how do you handle it? Ask yourself, would I buy this today at this price? If the answer is no, you've found the effect at work. We'll come back to that question in the second half, where we look at practical ways to price your own assets more honestly.

questions.explanation: She says you wouldn't pay more than three hundred.

title: Raising a Problem Early
script: Let's talk about a word that makes people nervous: escalation. Many students hear it and think, I'm telling the boss that someone has failed. But that's not what it is. Escalating simply means taking a problem to someone with more power to solve it. The best time to do it is early, not on the day everything breaks. Think about a delivery that's going to be two weeks late. If you say nothing, the customer will find out anyway, and your manager will find out last. That's the worst order. Now, how do you do it well? First, stick to the facts. Say, the shipment left the port four days late, and the new arrival date is the fifteenth. Don't say, the supplier is useless. Second, bring options. For example, we can pay for air freight, or we can move some stock from another warehouse. Third, say what you need: a decision by Friday. Nobody has ever been fired for being too clear, although I have seen a few people promoted for being unclear, which remains a mystery to me. When you share facts and options, you aren't blaming anyone. You're helping people decide. So next time you see a problem growing, don't wait and hope. Speak up while there is still time to choose.

title: What Executives Need to Hear
script: Imagine you're a passenger on a plane and the captain announces everything about the engines, the fuel flow and the wind speed. You'd probably start to worry. What you actually want to hear is: we're on course, there's turbulence ahead, and we'll land twenty minutes late. Senior leaders feel the same way about a planning update. They have little time and many topics, so give them three things. First, the decision: what exactly are you asking them to approve, and by when? State it at the beginning, not after ten slides. Second, the risk: what happens if nothing changes, and how likely is it? Put it in business terms, such as revenue at risk or patients without supply, rather than in planning jargon. Third, the options: usually two or three, each with a cost and a consequence, plus your recommendation. Leaders don't mind choosing, but they hate being handed a problem with no direction. Suppose a shortage threatens a launch. A weak update walks through every supplier delay. A strong one says: we need approval for air freight at fifty thousand, otherwise the launch slips by a month; here are the alternatives. Keep the details in an appendix, ready if somebody asks. In the next section, we'll look at how to rehearse the first sixty seconds.

title: Expired Stock Is an Old Decision
script: Finance sees a write-off in March: two hundred thousand in expired product, gone. The warehouse team says, it's just old stock. But if you ask a planner when that loss was decided, the honest answer is probably last July, or even earlier. That's why expiry is a planning failure that shows up months later. Stock doesn't expire by surprise. It expires because, at some point, we made more than we could sell, bought in bigger lots than we needed, or accepted product with a short life, and then we didn't notice until it was too late. Consider a simple chain. A forecast is too optimistic. Production makes the full amount. Sales falls short. The extra stock sits, month after month, and its remaining shelf life shrinks. By the time anyone looks, customers won't accept it. How do you prevent it? Look at stock by age, not just by quantity. Flag items that have more supply than their shelf life allows. Talk to sales early, when there is still time to promote or move the product. And review forecast accuracy honestly, because a bias towards optimism fills warehouses quietly. Who owns the write-off? Everyone who touched the decision. So the next time you see a number like that, don't ask who threw it away. Ask who made it, and why.

title: First Expired, First Out
script: Imagine two cartons of yogurt in your fridge. One expires tomorrow. One expires next week. Which do you eat first? The one that expires tomorrow, of course. Warehouses do the same thing, and the rule has a name: first expired, first out, or FEFO. Notice that it's not the same as first in, first out. FIFO looks at the day the goods arrived. FEFO looks at the date they expire. Those can be very different. A pallet that arrived last week might expire before one that arrived last month, if it was made earlier or has a shorter life. For anything with a shelf life, such as food, chemicals or medicines, FEFO is the safer rule. Now, shelf life also affects what you can sell. Many customers won't accept a product with less than, say, eighty percent of its life remaining. That means a product with three months left may be perfectly good and still unsellable to some customers. So stock with short remaining life is worth less, and eventually worth nothing. Nobody has ever come back from the far corner of a warehouse with good news about a forgotten pallet. To keep this under control, label clearly, check dates regularly, and tell sales early about stock getting close to the limit, so they can offer it before the date, not after.

title: Why a Tidy Workplace Matters
script: Walk into any well-run workplace and one thing strikes you before anything else: it's tidy. That isn't an accident. It's the result of a method called 5S, named after five Japanese words that we usually translate as sort, set in order, shine, standardize and sustain. Sort means you remove what you don't need. Set in order means everything has a place, and you can find it in seconds. Shine means you clean, and cleaning is also inspection, because you notice the leak or the crack. Standardize is making these rules visible and shared. Sustain is the hard one: keeping it up when the manager isn't looking. People often think 5S is about making the place look nice for visitors, but that's not the point. The point is to remove small frictions. Suppose a technician spends ten minutes a day looking for a torque wrench. Over two hundred days, that's more than thirty hours of one person's year gone. Multiply by a team, and you see the cost. Personally, I think 5S is the most underrated tool in lean, because it's cheap, it's fast, and it shows people that improvement is possible. Everything else in lean, from flow to quality, becomes much harder if the basics are a mess. Start with one shelf. Seriously, one shelf.

title: Do Our Adjustments Help
script: Every month, a statistical model produces a forecast. Then people get involved. Sales adjusts it up because a big deal might close. Marketing adjusts it for a campaign. Finance adjusts it to match the budget. Each of these changes feels sensible. But here's the question nobody asks often enough: did the change make the forecast better? That's what forecast value added measures. You compare the accuracy of each step. Is the adjusted forecast closer to actual demand than the statistical one? If yes, the step added value. If not, it added effort and, worse, error. In practice, teams often find an uncomfortable result: some adjustments help, and some make things worse. I can't give you numbers. The point is that you need to test your own. I remember a professor who used to say that an opinion is a hypothesis wearing a suit. Perhaps he was right. Anyway, back to the method. To run it, record the forecast at each stage, wait for the actuals, and compare the errors. Then decide where human judgment earns its place. Typically, it pays off for known events the model can't see, like a product launch or a competitor leaving the market. It rarely pays off for small, frequent tweaks made out of habit. If you can't show an adjustment helps, you should let the model speak.

title: Same Facts, Different Frames
script: Imagine two project updates. One says: the new process succeeds ninety percent of the time. The other says: the new process fails ten percent of the time. Same facts, exactly. Yet, as you can see in everyday life, listeners react very differently. The first sounds reliable and the second sounds worrying. This is framing: the way information is presented changes how it is judged, even when the content hasn't changed. In planning, you will meet it constantly. A supplier describes a delivery record as ninety-five percent on time, while your customer hears that one in twenty shipments is late. A forecast of plus five percent growth sounds fine, but a warning of a five percent shortfall against the target sounds like a problem. Is either description wrong? Not necessarily. But neither is neutral. Frames aren't wrong in themselves; the danger is not noticing them. So when you receive a number, translate it into the opposite frame and see whether your reaction changes. When you present a number, think about what you want your audience to understand, and choose a frame that is honest and doesn't hide the risk. Showing both versions side by side is often the fairest solution. If a figure feels especially comforting or especially alarming, that's a good moment to stop and ask how it was framed.

options: How information is presented can change how people judge it

questions.explanation: The same facts can sound reliable or worrying.

options: To introduce a new forecasting method

title: Why Plans Freeze Near Execution
script: There's a period in every plan when you stop changing it. Planners call it the frozen horizon, or the frozen window. Let's say it's four weeks. Inside those four weeks, production orders are fixed, materials are on their way, and people have been scheduled. Beyond four weeks, the plan can still change freely. Why freeze anything? Because every change close to execution causes a ripple. If you change an order for next Tuesday, the machine has to be reset, materials may need re-ordering, and the shift needs to be told. A change that looks small on a screen can mean overtime and waste on the floor. I once spent an entire train journey trying to open a window that was bolted shut. Frozen, you might say. Anyway, that's the idea. Of course, sometimes you have no choice. A key customer places an urgent order and the cost of saying no is higher than the cost of the disruption. So the freeze isn't absolute. It's a rule that makes people pay attention: changes inside the window need approval, and someone must say what it will cost. Without that rule, planners get a stream of small requests, each seeming reasonable, which together destroy any stability. The freeze doesn't exist to be rigid. It exists to make the price of changing the plan visible.

options: Plans should never be changed after they are made

Customers should not place urgent orders at all
Plans are fixed near execution because changes cost

title: Four Ways to Close a Gap
script: Suppose demand for next quarter is twelve thousand units and you can only make nine thousand. What do you do? In my experience, there are four moves, and good planners know all of them. First, speed up. Add a shift, pay for overtime, or ask a supplier to expedite. It works, but it costs money, and you can't do it forever. Second, shift. Move some demand to a later week, or move supply from another site. The customer waits a little, but nobody goes without. Third, ration. If you can't serve everyone, decide who gets priority. Maybe hospitals first, then large accounts, then the rest. This is uncomfortable, yet it's far better than letting the loudest customer win. Fourth, change the target. Sometimes the honest answer is that the plan was too ambitious, and you tell leadership that three thousand units won't be delivered this quarter. Some people find that conversation slightly less fun than a dentist appointment. Notice that these moves aren't exclusive. In the example, you might expedite one thousand units, shift one thousand to next quarter, and ration the remaining one thousand. The real skill is showing the options with their costs side by side, so the decision-makers can choose. Whenever you find a gap, don't just report it. Bring the options.

options: Overtime is the cheapest way to close a shortage

Nine thousand units
Three thousand units
Two thousand units

title: Feedback That Actually Helps
script: Imagine your friend is learning to cook, and you taste his soup. You could say, it's not good. That tells him nothing. Or you could say, I think it needs more salt, and the onions are still hard. Now he knows what to fix. Feedback at work is exactly like this. The best feedback has three qualities. It's specific, it's timely and it's about behaviour, not about the person. Let's start with specific. Don't say, you're not very organised. Say, in yesterday's meeting, the forecast file arrived ten minutes after we started, and we had to wait. See the difference? One is an opinion, the other is something both of you can see. Second, timely. Give feedback soon after the event, while both of you remember it. Feedback after six months is like a letter from the past. Third, behaviour. You can't change someone's personality, but you can ask for a different action next time. One good way to say it is: when this happened, the effect was this, and next time I'd like that. Finally, say something about what went well, but only if it's true. I think feedback is a gift, even when it feels uncomfortable, and giving it well is one of the kindest things a manager can do. So don't wait for the annual review. Do it this week.

title: When the Number Becomes the Goal
script: Suppose a warehouse is told that its target is ninety-eight percent of orders shipped on the day they arrive. That sounds sensible. Then something strange happens. The team notices that a hard order, one with a missing part, drags the figure down. So they quietly close the order as shipped and open a new one for the missing part. The number goes to ninety-nine percent, and customers wait just as long as before. That is a famous problem often summed up as, when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure. People are not cheating out of malice. They are responding rationally to what is rewarded. The number was only ever a stand-in for something we cared about, which was happy customers, and once it becomes the goal, we start serving the stand-in. Does that mean we should stop measuring? Certainly not. It means measuring more than one thing, so that gaming one is visible in another. Pair on-time shipping with the number of complaints, for example. It also means checking, from time to time, that the measure still reflects reality. Look at what people do, not just what they report. Frankly, I'm wary of any dashboard that shows only green, because real operations are never that tidy.

options: A ninety-eight percent target is much too low for most teams.
Employees who manipulate their figures should be dismissed at once.

questions.explanation: The speaker says the number is a stand-in for the goal.

questions.q: How did the warehouse team improve its figure?
options: It hired more workers for the day shift to speed things up.
It asked customers to accept later deliveries without complaint.

questions.explanation: The speaker says they closed the order as shipped and opened another for the missing part.

title: Leaving Without Leaving a Mess
script: I once worked with a colleague who went on holiday for three weeks and left one sentence: everything is in the shared folder. Everything was in the shared folder, along with four hundred other files and no clue which mattered. By day two, we were blocked on a supplier payment nobody knew how to release. That experience changed how I prepare for any absence. A good handover is not a data dump, it's a short, deliberate piece of writing for someone who has to act without calling you. So, what goes in it? First, what's in progress, with a status and the next step for each item, and deadlines clearly marked. Second, the decisions you expect to come up, and what you would decide, with your reasoning. Third, the people: who knows what, and who has authority to approve what. Fourth, the access and the routines that live only in your head, such as the report that must run every Monday before nine. Finally, name one backup and brief them in person, because a document alone rarely carries the nuance. I find it a little arrogant when people treat their own indispensability as a sign of success. If your team stops when you leave, you haven't built something strong, you've built a dependency. Try, then, to be easy to replace for a fortnight.

options: A short, clear handover lets colleagues keep working while you are away.

Managers should approve every action taken by the team during an absence.

questions.explanation: The speaker says a handover should help someone act without calling you.

options: A report for the manager
A delivery for a customer
