title: Levelling Instead of Chasing Orders
script: Suppose customers order very unevenly: eighty units on Monday, ten on Tuesday, a hundred and ten on Wednesday, and so on. The temptation is to follow the orders exactly. You work flat out on Wednesday, and then people stand around on Tuesday. That's called chasing demand, and it's exhausting and expensive. Heijunka, which means levelling, does the opposite. You look at the total demand over a longer period, say a week, and you produce roughly the same amount each day. If the week's total is three hundred units, you make sixty a day. The gap between production and orders is covered by a small buffer of finished goods. Think of a supermarket checkout. If the manager staffed it exactly to match the queue each minute, people would be running around one minute and idle the next. Instead, the store plans a steady number of cashiers for the busy period and accepts a small queue. Levelling also works on the mix: instead of making all of product A in the morning and all of product B in the afternoon, you alternate in small amounts. Why does it matter? A steady rhythm reduces overtime, stress and errors, and it makes your suppliers' lives easier too. So when a sudden spike appears in the order book, don't automatically add a shift. First, see if you can smooth it.

options: Production should match each day's orders exactly
Producing steadily beats following every order spike
Suppliers should deliver only on Wednesdays each week

questions.explanation: Heijunka smooths production instead of chasing demand.

options: Thirty units a day
Sixty units a day
One hundred and ten units a day
Eighty units a day
questions.explanation: A week's total of three hundred gives sixty a day.

options: To show that supermarkets avoid long queues

questions.explanation: Staffing minute by minute is like matching production to daily orders.

title: Why We Follow the Crowd
script: People often think that herd behaviour means people are foolish. But that's not quite right. Copying others is often a sensible shortcut. If a restaurant is full and the one next door is empty, you assume the full one is better. You don't have the information, but the crowd seems to have it. The problem begins when everybody does this at the same time. Think of a stock that rises because people see others buying it. More people buy, the price rises further, and nobody checks what the company is actually worth. Then one day the mood turns, and everyone leaves together. It happens in meetings too. Say a senior manager suggests cutting an order quantity. The next person agrees, and the third nods, even though she has a worry about a lead time. Each person is thinking, if nobody else sees a problem, perhaps I'm wrong. The result is a decision that looks unanimous but isn't really shared. As a new planner, you'll often be the least experienced person in the room, and that's exactly why your view matters. So how can you protect yourself? Write down your opinion before the discussion starts. Next, we'll look at how to raise a doubt politely when you're the only one with it.

questions.explanation: The speaker says copying is a sensible shortcut, but problems start when everybody does it.

Counting how many people agree
Asking the manager to speak last
Writing down your own opinion
questions.explanation: She advises writing down your opinion before the discussion starts.

To prove that restaurants are run better than most offices

title: Who Owns the Risk in Transit
script: A container of medical devices is sitting on a ship in the middle of the ocean, and a storm damages it. Who pays? You might say the shipping company. Often the real answer depends on the moment when the risk passed from seller to buyer. That moment is the idea behind delivery terms, which many people know as Incoterms. In plain language, these terms fix the exact point where the seller's responsibility ends and the buyer's begins. In some terms, that point is the seller's own factory gate. The buyer arranges everything from there. In others, the seller pays for transport to a named port, but risk still passes earlier, when the goods are loaded on the ship. In the most generous versions, the seller carries the risk right up to the buyer's door. Notice that cost and risk don't always change hands at the same place. That is the part that surprises people. A planner needs to care, because the point of transfer decides who must insure the goods, who deals with delays, and, crucially, when you can count the stock as yours. A shipment still at sea may be paid for but not yet in your hands. Next, we'll walk through three of the common terms using a map of one journey, so you can see exactly where each one draws the line.

options: Delivery terms mark where risk passes to the buyer
Containers are safer when they are loaded at a port

questions.explanation: She says the terms 'fix the exact point where the seller's responsibility ends and the buyer's begins.'

options: At the seller's factory gate
At the buyer's front door
At the port of arrival
When the goods are insured
questions.explanation: She says 'that point is the seller's own factory gate.'

questions.q: Why does the speaker begin with the damaged container?
options: To explain how medical devices are packed
To compare ships with other kinds of transport
To warn about storms during shipping seasons
To show why the point of transfer matters
questions.explanation: The opening question 'Who pays?' leads straight into the idea of when risk passes.

questions.q: What will the speaker probably do next?
options: Describe how storms damage large containers

title: Expanding the Pie
script: Consider a buyer and a supplier haggling over one thing: price. Every euro the buyer saves is a euro the supplier loses. Economists call that distributive bargaining, a fixed pie you merely cut differently. But real deals rarely have only one issue, and that's where the opportunity lies. Add payment terms, volumes, delivery timing, contract length. These matter differently to each side. Suppose the supplier is short of cash and would value payment in fifteen days instead of sixty far more than a small price reduction, while the buyer has low borrowing costs and can pay early without difficulty. By trading early payment for a lower price, both are better off than they'd be with a price fight alone. Similarly, a buyer who can commit to larger volumes in the quiet season helps the supplier's planning, and might receive a discount in return. I should mention that I once negotiated a contract in a restaurant where the waiter forgot our order three times, but that's a story for another day. Anyway, back to the point. The skill here is discovering what the other side values, and that means asking questions and listening, not guessing. Expanding the pie takes preparation: list your issues, rank them by importance to you, and estimate the ranking on the other side. When you walk into your next negotiation, don't ask how to win the price. Ask which other issues can create value.

options: Suppliers should always be paid after sixty days

Price is the only issue that matters in supplier deals

questions.explanation: Adding issues lets both sides gain.

questions.q: Why would the supplier value early payment?
options: It is short of cash
It plans to raise prices soon
It wants to sell larger volumes
It has high borrowing costs
questions.explanation: The talk says the supplier is short of cash.

questions.q: Why does the speaker mention the restaurant?
options: To give an example of a poor service contract
To show that restaurants negotiate better deals
To share a short tangent before returning
To explain distributive bargaining in detail
questions.explanation: She says it is a story for another day and returns to the point.

questions.q: What should a listener do before the next negotiation?
options: Avoid sharing any information with the other side
Offer early payment in every negotiation

questions.explanation: She advises ranking issues and estimating the other side's ranking.

title: Ask Why Before Arguing Price
script: A supplier says their price is final, one euro twenty per unit. Most of us start arguing about the price. We say it's too high, they say costs went up, and we end up in a stalemate. A better move is to ask why. A position is what someone says they want. An interest is the reason behind it. Maybe the supplier insists on one euro twenty because the raw material doubled in cost. Maybe it is because their other customers already pay that price and they fear a discount would leak. Or perhaps they have a cash problem and need money quickly. Each reason leads to a different solution. If it's cash flow, you could pay faster in return for a lower price. If it's a fear of leaks, you could agree on confidentiality, or a different packaging format that makes comparisons difficult. If it's the raw material, you might offer a longer contract with a price tied to an index. Did you notice that none of these ideas involve arguing about the price itself? That is how it works: when you ask a genuine question, you stop being an opponent and start solving a shared problem. And asking costs you nothing. So, next time, hold the argument about price for ten minutes, and ask first.

options: Raw material costs hardly ever change
Price is rarely important in supplier talks
Asking about the reasons behind a demand opens up solutions
Suppliers should lower prices when customers ask why
questions.explanation: The speaker contrasts positions with the interests behind them.

Buying more raw material for the supplier
Paying faster in return for a lower price
Agreeing to keep the prices confidential
questions.explanation: She says 'you could pay faster in return for a lower price'.

options: To check whether listeners remember the numbers
To point out the ideas avoid a fight over price
To criticize buyers who argue too much

questions.explanation: None of the ideas involve arguing about the price itself.

options: It works best with large suppliers
It is required by most contracts

questions.explanation: She says it ends in a stalemate and suggests asking first.

title: When Items Rarely Sell
script: Try to guess next month's sales from this history of a spare part: zero, zero, zero, four, zero, zero, one, zero, zero, zero, nine. If you take the average, you get about one and a half, but you will never sell one and a half. You will sell nothing, or a handful. That's intermittent demand: items that sell rarely and in an irregular pattern. They're common in spare parts, specialist products and the long tail of any catalog. Why do normal methods fail? Methods like moving averages assume demand is fairly steady and the errors are balanced. With many zeros, the forecast drifts up after a sale and down during the quiet periods, never matching reality. And the usual accuracy measures can behave strangely too, with a forecast of zero looking deceptively good. So what do planners do? They look at two things separately: how often a sale happens, and how large it is when it does. There are methods built on that idea, which you will meet later. In practice you also think about the cost of a missing part. If the part is cheap, hold a unit or two. If it is expensive and rarely needed, ask whether you can get it fast from a supplier instead of holding it. Do you really need stock of everything that might sell once a year? Often, the best answer is a policy, not a forecast.

options: How to price spare parts for large customers
Why catalogs should list far fewer products
Why ordinary methods fail for items that rarely sell
How to speed up deliveries from suppliers
questions.explanation: He defines intermittent demand and explains why 'normal methods fail.'

questions.q: Which two things do planners look at separately?
options: The cost of the part and the supplier's name
The season of the year and the sales region
The price of the part and its shelf life

questions.explanation: He says 'how often a sale happens, and how large it is when it does.'

options: To explain how accuracy measures work in practice
To show an average cannot represent rare sales
To show that the part sells steadily each month

title: Reading Inventory Turns Carefully
script: Let's talk about a number that managers love: inventory turns. It tells you how many times a year you sell and replace your whole stock. The calculation is simple. Take the cost of goods sold in a year, and divide it by the average value of inventory. If you sell twelve million a year and you hold two million on average, the turns are six. In other words, your stock is replaced every two months. A high number sounds great. Less cash is stuck on the shelf. But a high number can also hide a problem. Maybe the warehouse is nearly empty, and customers are waiting. A low number sounds bad, but a company may keep lots of stock on purpose, for example for slow, expensive spare parts that must be available immediately. And here is the big trap. Is it fair to compare a supermarket with an aircraft engine maker? Of course not. A supermarket may turn its stock thirty times a year, because food goes off. An engine maker may turn it twice. So compare only with similar companies, or with your own history. I'm a fan of this number, but only if it is used with care. Never judge it alone. Look at it next to service levels, and ask what the number is not telling you.

options: How supermarkets choose their main suppliers
How to calculate inventory turns and read them
Why spare parts should never be stored
How to increase annual sales by twelve million
questions.explanation: She explains the calculation and then the traps in reading it.

options: Two turns a year
Twelve turns a year
Six turns a year
Thirty turns a year
questions.explanation: She says 'the turns are six' for twelve million of sales and two million of stock.

questions.q: Why does the speaker compare a supermarket with an aircraft engine maker?
options: To argue that food is more valuable than machines
To explain how cost of goods sold is calculated
To show that turns differ between industries

questions.explanation: She says 'Of course not' to the comparison and gives thirty turns against two.

options: She thinks high turns are always best

title: When Low Stock Becomes Risky
script: Just-in-time means you keep very little stock. Materials arrive only when you need them, so you don't pay to store things, and you don't tie up cash. It saves a lot of money, and many companies built their success on it. But here's the catch. Low stock means low protection. Think about your own kitchen. If you buy food every day, your fridge is nearly empty, and you waste almost nothing. That's fine as long as the shop is open. If the shop closes for a week because of a storm, you have nothing for dinner. Someone who keeps a full cupboard is a little less efficient, but much safer. Business works the same way. Imagine a factory that holds only two days of a key component. If the supplier's truck is delayed by three days, the line stops. Every hour of that stop can cost far more than the storage would have cost in a year. So just-in-time isn't bad. It works well when deliveries are reliable and nearby. It becomes fragile when suppliers are far away, or when one source supplies everything. As a planner, you will often be asked to cut inventory. Before you agree, ask one question: what happens if the next delivery doesn't arrive?

options: Kitchens are the best place to learn planning

questions.explanation: The speaker says low stock means low protection.

options: Seven days

Two days
questions.explanation: The example factory holds only two days.

questions.q: Why does the speaker talk about a kitchen?
options: To explain how to reduce food waste
To suggest that planners should cook more
To compare keeping food with holding business inventory
To show that shops often close in storms
questions.explanation: A near-empty fridge works like low stock.

title: Pull Signals Instead of Forecasts
script: Most planning starts with a forecast: we guess what will be needed, then push material toward the customer. Kanban turns this around. Instead of guessing, you wait for a signal that something has actually been consumed, and only then do you replace it. The word means card in Japanese, and the classic version is exactly that: a card attached to a bin. When the bin is empty, the card goes back to the supplier, or to the previous process, and it triggers a refill of that precise quantity. Nothing is made or ordered without a real signal. I once worked with a plant where the bolts on the line were supplied by kanban, two bins per station. When one bin ran out, the worker flipped to the other one, and a runner took the empty bin to the store. For years, they never had a bolt shortage. That's the appeal. But pull works best under certain conditions. Demand has to be fairly steady, lead times short, and the items cheap and used often. For rare or highly variable items, a signal arrives too late, and you're better off forecasting. So the question isn't whether kanban is good, but where it fits. Having seen how a simple signal replaces a guess, we can now compare the two approaches on a product with lumpy demand.

title: Planning a Launch With No History
script: Forecasting a new product is like cooking for guests when you don't know how hungry they are. There is no past data to look at. You are guessing, so the question is how to be wrong safely. Two risks pull in opposite directions. Make too much, and you're left with stock that may expire or need a discount. Make too little, and the first customers find empty shelves, just when everyone is watching. Which is worse depends on the product. For a medicine that patients need, running out is a serious problem. For a fashion item, extra stock is the greater danger. A practical approach is to build up in stages. Start with a smaller first batch, based on a careful estimate, perhaps using sales of a similar product. Then watch real orders for the first few weeks, and adjust the next batch. Keep some flexibility: agree with your suppliers that they can increase volume quickly if sales are strong. And work together with sales and marketing, because they know what promotions, trial offers and advertising are planned. Don't forget that the first weeks are often unusual. Some customers fill their shelves at the start, and then reorder less. So don't read the first orders as the real long-term demand. Wait for the pattern to settle.

title: Why the Average Can Mislead
script: Here's a puzzle. Two suppliers both have an average lead time of ten days. Most students tell me they're equal. They aren't. Supplier A always delivers in nine, ten or eleven days. Supplier B sometimes delivers in four days, and sometimes in eighteen. The average is the same. But the experience is very different. With A, you can plan: you know the goods will arrive around day ten. With B, you must prepare for the worst case. If you plan for ten days and the truck comes on day eighteen, you run out of stock. If you plan for eighteen, you carry a lot of extra inventory most of the time. Either way, B costs you money. That is why the average lead time matters less than how much it moves around. Planners call that variability. Now, here's a question for you. Would you rather have a train that is always ten minutes late, or one that is sometimes on time and sometimes an hour late? Most of us prefer the first. We can work around a steady delay. We cannot work around a surprise. So when you compare suppliers, ask for the range, not just the average. Look at the real delivery history, and judge the supplier by the spread.

title: Two Clocks Often Confused
script: Ask three people in a meeting what lead time means and you'll get four answers. That's not a criticism. It's just how language works when nobody bothers to check. So let's fix it. Lead time is what the customer, or the next step, experiences: the time from placing an order to receiving the goods. Cycle time is what the process spends actually working on one unit: the time from starting the work to finishing it. Take a bakery that needs forty minutes to bake a loaf. Forty minutes is the cycle time. But if the order arrives on Monday and the oven is booked until Wednesday morning, the customer waits two days and forty minutes. That is the lead time, and most of it is waiting. Now, why does this matter for planning? Imagine a planner who types the cycle time into a system field called lead time. Every order will then look as though it arrives in forty minutes, and the plan will promise things nobody can deliver. I've seen spreadsheets that were, shall we say, optimistic about physics. The reverse mistake is just as costly. Use the full lead time to judge how fast a machine runs, and you'll buy equipment you don't need. So here's the rule. If the question is how long the customer waits, use lead time. If the question is how fast the process works, use cycle time. Never swap them quietly.

title: Why Long Queues Mean Long Waits
script: What happens to waiting time if you double the amount of work you allow into a system, but the team still finishes the same amount each day? Most people guess it gets a bit longer. In fact, it doubles. This is Little's law, and the idea is simple. The number of items in the system equals the rate they leave multiplied by the time they spend inside. Let me use a queue to show it. Say your team has thirty requests waiting, and it completes ten requests per day. Let's work out how long a new request waits. Thirty divided by ten, so three days. Now suppose your colleagues keep adding requests, and the queue grows to sixty. The team is working just as hard, still ten a day, but the new request waits six days. Nobody got slower. There was just more work in progress. This gives you two ways to shorten the wait. You can raise the speed of completing work, which is usually hard, or you can limit how much work enters at one time. Most teams find the second one much easier. It feels strange to say no to new requests. Yet that is how the queue shrinks. Next time a customer complains about delays, check how much work is waiting before you ask people to work faster.

title: Winning Every Point and Losing
script: Suppose you've just negotiated a contract with your most important supplier. You pushed on price, on payment terms, on penalties, and you got nearly everything. Congratulations. Did you win? It depends on what happens next. A supplier you will need for ten years is not an opponent you meet once. It is a partner whose goodwill you will use on the worst days: when a shortage hits, when a batch fails, when you need an urgent shipment at no notice. The first call back goes to the customer who was tough but fair, not to the one who squeezed every cent. Suppliers have memories. If you leave them with a margin so thin that they lose money on your business, they will cut corners, delay your orders behind more profitable ones, or look for a way out at the first chance. Consider a case: a buyer pushes the price down eight percent and wins. A year later, the supplier misses deliveries and quality slips, and the buyer spends more fixing problems than the saving was worth. What matters more than how much you can get today is what kind of relationship you want in year five. Aim for a deal both sides can live with and defend internally. Be firm on what matters, give where it costs you little, and leave the other side with a reason to try hard for you.

title: Why Losses Feel Bigger
script: Would you rather get one hundred euros, or lose one hundred euros? Silly question. Now think about a coin toss: heads you win one hundred and ten, tails you lose one hundred. On average, this is a good deal. Yet most people refuse. Why? Because a loss hurts more than the same gain feels good. This is called loss aversion, and it is often much stronger than people expect. In business, it shapes decisions every day. A manager avoids switching to a new supplier, even a cheaper one, because the possible loss, a delivery problem, feels bigger than the saving. A planner keeps extra stock because running out feels worse than paying a little to store it. A team holds on to a product that is losing money, because dropping it feels like admitting a loss. None of this is crazy. It's human. But it does mean we are often more careful than the numbers suggest. Here's what you can do. Write the possible gains and losses as plain numbers, side by side, and ask whether you'd accept the same deal if it were presented the other way around. Understanding this bias won't make you a robot, which is probably a relief to all of us. It just helps you notice when fear, not facts, is steering.

title: Make It Ourselves or Buy It In
script: A company often has to decide whether to manufacture a component itself or buy it from a supplier. It sounds like a question of price, but price alone rarely settles it. Let me walk through three factors. The first is cost, and the trap here is comparing only the unit price. In-house production carries fixed costs, such as equipment and skilled staff, that don't disappear when volumes fall. A supplier turns those fixed costs into variable ones, which is attractive when demand is uncertain. The second factor is control. If a part determines the quality of your product, or contains know-how that sets you apart, you may want to keep it close. Hand it over, and you also hand over some of your ability to react quickly when something goes wrong. The third is risk. Relying on one supplier exposes you to their problems, whether it's a factory fire or a strike. Yet producing in-house exposes you to your own problems, and these are no smaller. So is there a rule? Hardly. A sensible approach is to keep what is strategic and hard to copy, and to buy what is standard and easy to source from several companies. Whatever you decide, treat it as a decision to be revisited. Markets, volumes and technology change, and yesterday's right answer can become tomorrow's expensive habit.

title: Helping Your Boss Decide
script: Let me start with a story. I once worked with a manager who got the same email from two planners. The first said, we have a supply problem, what should we do? The second said, we have a supply problem, here are two options, and I recommend the second one. Guess which planner got an answer in five minutes. That's what managing up really means. It doesn't mean flattering your boss. It means making their decision easier. Your manager is busy and has many problems on their desk. So don't hand them yours without help. Give them a short summary, two or three options, and your own recommendation. For example, option A is to switch to air freight, which costs ten thousand dollars and saves one week. Option B is to wait, which is free but risks missing the deadline. I recommend A, because the customer contract has a penalty. See how that works? You've done the thinking. Your boss only needs to say yes or no. Some students think a recommendation is arrogant. I think it's respectful, because it shows you took the problem seriously. If your boss disagrees, you'll learn how they think. Either way, you win. So the next time you need a decision, send options and a clear recommendation, and watch how much faster things move.

title: Wrong Both Ways or Always One Way
script: Two planners each forecast one hundred units a month for a year. Planner A is wrong by about twenty units every month, sometimes high, sometimes low. Planner B is also wrong by twenty, but always on the high side. Who is the better forecaster? Honestly, you might say they are equal, because the average error size is the same. That error size is what we call accuracy, and a common way to measure it is MAPE, the mean absolute percentage error. But there's a second idea: bias. Bias asks whether your errors lean in one direction. Planner A has almost no bias. The mistakes cancel each other out over time. Planner B has a strong bias. Every month, there are twenty units too many, and over the year that's two hundred and forty extra units in the warehouse. Why does it matter? Random error is hard to remove, so we cover it with safety stock. But bias is a pattern, and patterns can be fixed. If you know you always overestimate by twenty percent, you can just adjust. So measure both. Accuracy tells you how big your mistakes are. Bias tells you whether they have a direction. If they do, someone should find out why, and fix the habit, not the number.

title: One Wrong Field, Months of Damage
script: Consider a single field in your system: the unit of measure on one raw material. Somebody enters it as boxes of ten when the supplier actually sells it in boxes of one hundred. It seems trivial. But now follow the consequences. The planning engine, which has no common sense whatsoever, believes it needs ten times fewer boxes than it really does. Orders go out for the wrong quantities. Shortages appear, expediting begins, and a planner spends a Friday evening rebooking freight. The field stays wrong, so the same mistake repeats every cycle. Months pass before anyone traces it back, because by then the symptom, a shortage, looks nothing like the cause, a typo. Think of a supermarket where the price tag under the cheese is wrong. Every shopper who scans that cheese is charged incorrectly, and the store only discovers the problem when the accounts don't add up weeks later. The error didn't multiply by itself; the volume of transactions did the multiplying. Master data works the same way. It's the foundation that every automated decision stands on. So treat it with the discipline you'd give a financial record. Assign an owner to each critical field, validate changes before they take effect, and audit a sample regularly. If you only remember one thing, remember that bad orders are usually symptoms, and the cure often lies upstream in a field nobody has looked at for years.

title: Forecasting With a Fading Memory
script: A forecast built on history has to answer one question: how much should yesterday count compared with last year? A moving average gives a simple answer. Take the last, say, three months of sales, add them up, divide by three, and that is next month's forecast. Each month in the window has equal weight, and anything older is ignored completely. It's easy to understand and it smooths out noise. The weakness is that it reacts slowly when demand really changes, and the oldest month drops out suddenly, which can make the forecast jump. Exponential smoothing tweaks the idea. It also uses past data, but recent months count the most, and the weight fades gradually as you go back. Nothing is dropped suddenly. People often think exponential smoothing is a much more advanced method, but the idea is just a moving average with fading memory. You choose how fast the memory fades. If it fades quickly, the forecast follows recent changes closely, but it also follows random noise. If it fades slowly, the forecast is stable, but slow to react. There's no perfect setting. Frankly, I'm always a bit suspicious when someone sells a forecasting tool as magic. Underneath, most of them are using one of these two ideas. Understand them, and you can judge the tool, instead of the other way around.

title: Small Changes, Better Choices
script: A nudge is a small change in how a choice is presented that steers people toward a better decision, without forbidding anything. The classic example is the default. Take expense reports. If people have to tick a box to choose the economy fare, many will pick the flexible one. If economy is already selected, most will leave it. Nobody has been told what to do, and the savings add up. Now think about our own world. Say planners have to enter a reason code when they override a forecast. If the first option on the list is simply other, you'll see other everywhere. Put the real reasons first, make them specific, and the data suddenly becomes useful. Another nudge is a short reminder at the right moment, such as a message the day before the monthly close. It doesn't take much, and I'm told it's far cheaper than a reorganisation. Notice what these have in common. They're easy to reverse and they respect people's freedom. If a nudge needs a long explanation or a penalty, it has stopped being a nudge. In the next part of the webinar, we'll go through how to test one, using a simple before-and-after comparison. The take-away: before you write a new rule, ask whether a better default would do the job.

title: What You Give Up When You Choose
script: Ask most people what a decision costs, and they'll say, the price. But economists give a different answer. The true cost of a choice is the value of the best alternative you gave up. This is called opportunity cost, and it's the reason behind a lot of good and bad decisions. Here is a simple example. Suppose a planner spends a whole Friday manually fixing a spreadsheet. The salary cost is clear. But the opportunity cost is whatever else she could have done with that day, perhaps building an automatic report that would save five hours every week for a year. Nobody sees that invoice, and yet it's the larger one. The same logic works for money. If a company keeps a million euros of extra stock, it pays for storage, yes, but it also loses what that million could earn if invested elsewhere. The cost isn't on any bill, so it's easy to ignore. Isn't it strange how we worry about spending money but not about wasting choices? I think this is one of the most useful ideas in business, because it forces you to compare, not just approve. So before you say yes to a project, ask: what are we not doing because of this? If the answer makes you uncomfortable, that's valuable information.

title: Reading OTIF Numbers Carefully
script: A supplier tells you their OTIF is ninety-five percent. A second supplier says eighty-two. Which one is better? You can't know yet. OTIF stands for on time, in full. An order line counts as a success only if it arrives by the agreed date and with the complete quantity. If either condition fails, the line fails. Let's use numbers. Say a supplier ships one hundred lines in a month. Ninety arrive on the right day, but only eighty-five of those carry the full quantity. That's eighty-five percent. People often think OTIF measures how good a supplier is overall, but it only measures how well they match one particular definition. Now, here's the thing. A tough definition can hide good performance. If a customer counts a delivery as late when it arrives one day early, or as short when it's missing one box in a thousand, the number drops, even though the service is quite good. Another customer might allow a window of two days and a tolerance of two percent. Same supplier, much higher score. Frankly, comparing two OTIF numbers without checking the rules is pointless, and I find it quite annoying how often it happens. So before you compare, ask three things. What counts as on time? What counts as in full? And is it measured by line, order or quantity?

options: Suppliers should be dropped when OTIF falls below ninety
Early deliveries are always better than late ones

questions.explanation: The speaker says to check the rules before comparing scores.

options: Eighty-five percent
Ninety-five percent
Eighty-two percent
Ninety percent

title: Cleaning History Without Losing It
script: Your sales history has a spike in June. Three times the normal volume. A planner sees it and thinks, that's an outlier, let me delete it. Is that always the right thing to do? Not at all. First, ask what caused it. If the spike came from a one-off event, such as a customer buying out the stock for a single project, then yes, clean it. Left in, it would push your forecast up for no reason. But if the spike came from a promotion that you run every year, then deleting it erases information you'll need again. The better approach is to separate the two parts of the sales: the baseline, which is what you'd sell without any promotion, and the promotional lift, which is the extra volume because of it. Then you forecast the baseline from history and add the lift when the next promotion is planned. A data error is different again. A missing delivery, a duplicate order, or a unit mistake should be corrected whenever you find it. So the rule isn't, remove outliers. It's, explain outliers. Keep a short note beside each cleaned point, saying what happened and why you changed it. Months later, nobody will remember, and the next planner will need the story as much as the number.

questions.explanation: She defines it as 'the extra volume because of it.'

questions.explanation: She answers 'Not at all' and explains when deleting erases useful information.

title: Why Our Ranges Are Too Narrow
script: Let me start with a small experiment. Suppose I ask you for the monthly demand of a product, and I want a range where you're ninety percent sure the real number will fall. Most people give a range that's far too tight. When researchers check, the real answer lands inside those so-called ninety percent ranges only about half the time. That's overconfidence. We know a lot, so we feel we know more than we do. Here's an example from planning. A planner says next month's orders will be between one thousand and one thousand two hundred units. It sounds precise and professional. Then orders come in at one thousand five hundred, and everyone is surprised. But the range was never wide enough to be honest. A better habit is to ask: what is the lowest number that wouldn't shock me, and the highest? Then widen both ends, because you probably started too narrow. Why does this matter for your teams? Because a narrow range sets a very small safety stock, and then every small surprise becomes a shortage. Now, this is just the first half of the picture. After the break we'll practise building honest ranges from past forecast errors. The take-away: if your ninety percent range never surprises you, it's probably not a ninety percent range.

questions.explanation: She says it lands inside 'only about half the time'.

title: Fixing the Few Causes That Matter
script: Here is an idea that can save you weeks of work. In many situations, about eighty percent of the problems come from about twenty percent of the causes. It's called the Pareto principle. The numbers are not exact, but the pattern is very common. Let me show you with an example. A distribution centre had one hundred complaints last month. When they sorted them, thirty-five were damaged boxes, thirty were wrong labels, and the rest were spread over eleven small causes: late trucks, missing papers, and so on. So two causes created sixty-five percent of the trouble. If the team had tried to fix all thirteen causes at once, they would have needed months. Instead, they changed the box type and added a label scan. In six weeks, complaints dropped by half. That's the power of looking at the biggest few first. How do you do it? Count the problems, group them by cause, and sort from largest to smallest. Then draw a simple bar chart. Sorry, I'm getting ahead of myself, and I know a bar chart sounds basic. Back to what I was saying: the chart shows you where to start. Remember that the biggest cause is not always the easiest one to fix, so check the effort, too. But if you only have time for one action, you now know where to aim.

questions.explanation: The speaker explains that a few causes create most of the trouble.

options: It replaced all of the delivery trucks used by its drivers.

title: Why Projects Run Late
script: Ask a team how long a project will take, and they'll give you a date. Ask the same team how long similar projects took in the past, and the answer is almost always longer. This gap has a name: the planning fallacy. We build our plans from the best-case story in our heads, where every task goes smoothly, nobody gets sick, and no supplier is late. We forget the delays that always happen in real projects. I once worked with a team installing a new warehouse system. They estimated twelve weeks. Three earlier installations at the company had taken nineteen, twenty-two and twenty-one weeks, but the team felt this one was different, because they were more experienced. It finished in twenty. The solution is to look at the outside view. Instead of asking how long this project will take, ask how long projects like it actually took. Take the median of past cases, here about twenty-one weeks, and use it as your starting point. Then adjust it only for real, specific differences, not for optimism. Also, add a buffer, and separate it from individual tasks so that people don't use it up early. Finally, record your actual durations after every project, because without data you can't correct anything. So, next time someone presents a confident timeline, ask for the history behind it.

options: Plans are too optimistic, so past data should guide estimates

Warehouse systems should take twelve weeks

questions.explanation: The solution is to use the outside view of similar projects.

options: Nineteen weeks
Twelve weeks
Twenty-two weeks
Twenty weeks
questions.explanation: The speaker says 'It finished in twenty.'

options: To show past data contradicted the team's estimate
To explain how warehouse systems are installed
To praise the team's long experience

title: When Planning Settings Go Stale
script: Every planning system has settings. Lead time, minimum order quantity, lot size. We type them in once, and then we forget them. That's the problem. These numbers go stale quietly, and nobody notices until something breaks. Let me give you an example. The system says a supplier needs four weeks to deliver. So it tells us to order four weeks before we need the goods. But last year the supplier moved to a new factory, and now the real time is six weeks. Every order arrives two weeks late, and we keep running short. Nobody changed the system, so planners start adding their own extra buffer by hand. I once worked with a team that did this for almost two years. Each planner had a private rule, and nobody could explain the numbers. When they finally checked, half the settings were wrong. The same thing happens with minimum order quantities. If a supplier lowers the minimum from one thousand to five hundred, but the system still says one thousand, you buy too much and pay to store it. So make a habit. Once every quarter, compare the system with real deliveries. Next, I'll show you a simple way to do that check in about an hour.

title: Designing Errors Out of the Process
script: Have you ever tried to put the wrong fuel in your car? If you drive a diesel, the pump nozzle for petrol is usually too wide to fit. You can't make the error even if you're tired or distracted. That's poka-yoke, a Japanese term for mistake-proofing. The idea is to design the process so that the error is either impossible or immediately obvious, instead of telling people to be more careful. Telling people to be careful doesn't work for long. Everyone gets tired. Let's look at a planning example. Suppose planners enter order quantities by hand, and every few months someone adds a zero by accident, turning one hundred into one thousand. You could send a reminder email. Or you could set a system rule so that any quantity more than five times the usual order needs a confirmation. Better still, you could use a dropdown with approved quantities. Notice the difference in attitude: the first blames the person, the second fixes the process. There are two flavors. Prevention stops the mistake from happening. Detection flags it right away, before it moves downstream. Prevention is better, but detection is often cheaper. If you leave this lecture remembering one thing, make it this: when you find a mistake, don't ask who did it. Ask what allowed it.

options: Orders should always be approved by two managers

questions.explanation: Poka-yoke makes the error impossible or obvious.

questions.explanation: The speaker says such a quantity 'needs a confirmation'.

title: How to Say 'I See It Differently'
script: Disagreeing at work isn't rude. Staying silent while a bad idea goes ahead is much worse. The skill is to challenge the idea without attacking the person. So here is a simple structure. Step one: acknowledge. I can see why you suggest that, or that's a useful point. It shows you listened. Step two: state your concern about the idea, not the person. Say, my worry is that the lead time might be too long, rather than you haven't thought about lead times. Step three: offer something. What if we tested it with one supplier first? That moves the conversation from a fight to a problem to solve. A few phrases help. I see it slightly differently. Could we look at it from another angle? Have we considered the cost of delay? Notice they're soft, but they're not weak. The words but and however can sound sharp, so try and instead. I understand the goal, and I'd like to check the risk before we start. Now, I'm told that in some meetings simply saying actually will start a three-hour debate, so use it carefully. The respect is in the tone as much as the words. Stay calm, ask real questions, and be ready to be persuaded yourself. If you can change your mind in public, people will take your disagreement seriously.

questions.explanation: The speaker gives acknowledge, concern and offer as a structure.

options: Using 'actually' to start the sentence

Using 'and' to connect your concern
questions.explanation: She says to try 'and' instead of 'but' or 'however'.

title: Now Beats Later, Almost Every Time
script: Offer someone a hundred pesos today or one hundred and ten next week, and many will take the hundred today. Offer the same choice a year from now, and suddenly they'll wait the extra week. That flip is called present bias: we give too much weight to the immediate reward and too little to the later one. It explains why saving for retirement feels abstract. A thousand pesos spent on dinner is vivid, while a thousand pesos in thirty years is a rumour. The practical fix is to take the decision out of the moment. Set up an automatic transfer on payday, so the money is gone before the present self can object. The same bias shows up at work. A planner knows a recurring data error is wasting two hours a week, but fixing it takes a full day. Today's urgent request always wins, and the fix is postponed again. Personally, I admire how consistently my future self is expected to be more disciplined than I am. If you notice yourself postponing a fix, book it in the calendar now, as a fixed appointment, and protect it like a customer meeting. Small, scheduled commitments beat good intentions. The take-away: don't rely on your future self to be more patient, design today's decision so that patience is already built in.

title: Answering a Supplier Price Increase
script: A supplier writes: from next month, our prices go up eight percent. What now? Many people think there are only two choices, accept or refuse. But there is a lot of room in between. Start with questions. What is driving the increase? Is it materials, energy, labor? Does it apply to all customers, or only to us? When does it take effect? Then ask for evidence. A serious supplier should be able to show how their costs changed, even if they hide some details. If the increase comes from a cost that is falling now, that is a strong argument. Next, think about options short of accepting. You can ask for a smaller increase, or a later start date, so you have time to adjust your own prices. You can offer a longer contract or larger volumes in return for a lower rise. You can also check the market quietly, because a second quote tells you whether eight percent is normal. Finally, look at your side of the table: could you change the specification, or reduce waste, to lower the total cost? Notice that nothing here requires an argument. It requires preparation, patience and a calm tone. Keep records, too, so next year you can see how this supplier's prices moved. And remember, the first letter is rarely the last word.

title: Who Does What
script: Let me tell you about a project where everybody was sure somebody else was handling the supplier audit. I once worked with a team where three people did the same report on the same day, and nobody sent the audit schedule at all. That's the double problem of unclear roles: duplicated work and dropped tasks. One simple tool that fixes both is called RACI. It stands for responsible, accountable, consulted and informed. Responsible means the person who does the work. Accountable means the one who owns the result, and there should be only one name here. Consulted people give input before a decision, and informed people hear about it after. You make a small table. The tasks go down the side, the people go across the top, and each box gets a letter. Let's say the task is approving a new packaging supplier. The buyer is responsible, the procurement head is accountable, quality is consulted, and the warehouse is informed. Now everybody knows what to do, and who to ask. Honestly, I find it hard to understand why more teams don't do this, because it takes about twenty minutes. The common mistake is to put two As on one task. If two people are accountable, nobody is. Keep it simple, review it at the start of each project, and you'll save yourself a lot of confusion.

options: Project tables should list every task on a separate page.

questions.explanation: The speaker says RACI fixes duplicated work and dropped tasks.

options: Nobody at all

title: Setting the Trigger for Reordering
script: Let's work with one product: printer paper in an office. You use twenty boxes a week, which is four a day. The supplier needs five days to deliver. So during the wait, you'll use five times four, twenty boxes. That number, twenty, is your demand during lead time. If you order when exactly twenty boxes are left, the new boxes arrive just as the last one is used. Perfect, on paper. But real demand is not always four a day. Some days it's six. Some weeks the supplier takes seven days instead of five. So we add a buffer. Let's say ten extra boxes. Now the reorder point is thirty. When the stock falls to thirty, you place the order. That's the whole idea: reorder point equals demand during lead time plus a safety buffer. The more unpredictable the demand or the delivery, the bigger the buffer. And no, a bigger buffer for everything isn't the answer. It's a calculation, not a feeling. I once saw a team set every reorder point to "a lot", which is a number only in the loosest sense. Try it with one of your own items this week. Pick something you buy often, find the daily use and the delivery time, and see what you get. Then compare the answer with the point you use today.

options: How to work out the stock level at which you reorder
How to negotiate shorter delivery times with suppliers
How to forecast weekly demand for new products
Why office supplies need a different policy from other goods
questions.explanation: He builds the reorder point step by step from lead-time demand plus a buffer.

questions.q: In the example, how many boxes are used during the five-day wait?
options: Four boxes
Ten boxes
Twenty boxes
Thirty boxes
questions.explanation: He says 'you'll use five times four, twenty boxes.'

questions.q: Why does the speaker say 'a lot' is a number 'only in the loosest sense'?
options: To praise the team for being flexible about numbers
To explain how variability is measured by teams
To show that numbers cannot be used for reorder points
To joke that a team's method was too vague
questions.explanation: He contrasts the vague 'a lot' with 'a calculation, not a feeling.'

questions.q: What does the speaker imply about the team that set every reorder point to 'a lot'?
options: Their method had no real basis

title: A Risk Register That Gets Used
script: A risk register is a list of things that might go wrong, and what you plan to do about them. Simple enough. Yet most registers I've seen are written once, filed away and never opened again. So let's make one that works. Each risk needs four things. First, likelihood: how probable is it? Use a simple scale, low, medium or high. Second, impact: if it happens, how bad is it? Same scale. Third, an owner, a named person, not a department, who watches this risk. Fourth, the action that reduces it. Let's take a single supplier of a key ingredient. Likelihood: medium. Impact: high, because production would stop. Owner: Marco from procurement. Action: qualify a second supplier by March. Notice that the action is something you can do, not just a hope. Then review the register briefly at every monthly meeting, and focus on the red items, the ones with high likelihood and high impact. I'm honestly a fan of this tool. In my view, a register is not about being pessimistic. It's about being able to say, calmly, we saw this coming. I've never had a project with zero risks, though a few have claimed it, usually just before something went wrong. Keep the list short and alive, and it'll earn its place.

options: Risks should be listed once and then stored in a safe place.

title: Treating the Cause, Not the Symptom
script: Picture a warehouse where the same shelf runs empty every Friday. Each time, someone drives to the supplier, picks up an emergency batch and the problem disappears. Everyone feels like a hero. Then, next Friday, it happens again. That is what happens when you fix a symptom. You remove the pain but not the reason for it. To find the root cause, a useful trick is to ask why five times. Why is the shelf empty? Because the delivery arrived late. Why late? Because the order was sent on Thursday. Why Thursday? Because the system only sends orders after the weekly review. Why does the review happen on Thursday? Because that is when the manager is free. Now we've found something we can change: the ordering schedule. By the fifth why, you usually stop talking about people and begin talking about process. Incidentally, I read recently that some airlines save money by removing one olive from the salad. Anyway, back to the point. The point is that quick fixes have a place, but only while you work on the real one. If you're solving the same problem repeatedly, you aren't solving it. Next time something recurs, resist the urge to patch it again, and set aside an hour to ask why until the answer is something you can actually change.

title: The Cushion Between Plan and Reality
script: Let's start with a simple question. Why do we keep safety stock? Because the world doesn't follow the forecast. Demand goes up without warning, or a supplier delivers three days late. Safety stock is the extra inventory we hold for those surprises. Think of it as a small cushion between the plan and reality. Now, how big should the cushion be? That depends on the service level you want. Say you want to have a product available ninety-five times out of a hundred. To reach ninety-nine, you need much more stock, not just a little more. The last few percent are very expensive. Here's an example. For one item, moving from ninety-five to ninety-nine percent might double the safety stock. And every box on the shelf is cash that you can't use for anything else. It can also expire, get damaged or just get in the way. Some people say the perfect warehouse is full of everything. Those people are not paying for it. So more is not always safer. Too much stock can hide problems, like late suppliers, instead of solving them. I would rather ask: what exactly are we protecting against? If the answer is unclear, the number is probably wrong. The take-away: choose the service level on purpose, and then pay only for the cushion that you really need.

title: The Power of 'I Don't Know'
script: Most of us were taught that saying I don't know in a meeting looks weak. In my experience, the opposite is true. The weak move is guessing. Say a director asks you what the inventory level will be at the end of the quarter, and you aren't sure. If you invent a number, there's a good chance you'll be wrong, and then people stop trusting every other number you give. So how do you say it well? First, be direct, not apologetic. Say, I don't have that figure in front of me. Skip the long explanation. Second, show what you do know: I can tell you the current stock is stable, but the incoming batch is still uncertain. Third, and this is the key, promise a follow-up with a time. I'll send you the number by four o'clock today. Then do it. That last step is what makes the whole thing credible. People remember whether you came back, not whether you knew at that moment. Of course, if you say I don't know to every question, people may start to wonder what exactly you do. But used honestly, it's one of the strongest things a professional can say. As a team lead, you should also let your people say it safely. If they fear punishment for it, you'll get confident answers that are wrong, which is a very expensive kind of confidence.

title: A Polite and Firm No
script: Saying no is hard, especially at work. We worry about offending a colleague, a customer or a boss. But if you say yes to everything, you eventually fail at something, and that damages trust far more than an honest refusal. The trick is to say no to the request, not to the person. Here are three techniques. First, explain briefly. Not a long apology, just a reason: I can't take that on this week because the quarter-end report is due. Second, offer an alternative. I can't do it by Friday, but I could do it by Tuesday. Or: I can't build the whole analysis, but I can send you the data. Third, keep your tone warm and your message firm. Don't say maybe when you mean no, because maybe leaves the other person waiting and hoping. Small digression: I once had a manager who answered every request with the phrase let me think about it, and then never answered. We called it the slow no. Anyway, back to the point. Suppose a customer asks for delivery in two days and you can manage five. You could say: two days isn't possible, but I can guarantee five, and I can ship half the order earlier. The customer hears a plan rather than a refusal. A good no, delivered kindly, actually builds respect, because people learn that your yes means something.

title: When There Is Too Little Time or Money
script: Think about the last time you had a deadline in two hours. What happened to your attention? It probably became very narrow. You stopped noticing anything else: emails, lunch, even a colleague saying hello. Researchers describe this as the scarcity mindset. When we have too little of something, whether it's time, money or energy, our mind locks onto that shortage. This can be useful for a short sprint, but it has a hidden cost. Imagine you're shopping with a very small budget. You're so focused on today's bills that you forget to compare prices on things you buy every month, so you pay more over time. The same thing happens at work. A planner with three urgent tasks may ignore the quiet problem that will create ten urgent tasks next month. It's like driving in heavy traffic: you only look at the car in front, and you miss the road sign telling you the exit is coming. So what does this mean for managers? Don't judge people harshly for short-term thinking when they're overloaded. Instead, give them some slack. A little free time or a small buffer lets people think ahead again. To finish this part, let's see how teams can create that slack in a real schedule.

title: Preparing for More Than One Future
script: Most of us plan with one number. One forecast, one budget, one story about next year. The trouble is that the future rarely follows the story. Scenario planning is a different habit. Instead of betting on one future, you prepare two or three plausible ones. Say you run distribution for a medical device company. Scenario one: demand grows at the expected pace. Scenario two: a competitor leaves the market and your volumes jump by thirty percent. Scenario three: a port strike delays imports by a month. For each one, you ask three questions. What would we see first? What would we do? And what must we prepare now? I once worked with a logistics manager who kept a one-page sheet for each scenario in her desk drawer. When a strike did happen, she took out the page, and her team was moving within the hour while others were still arguing. Notice that you don't need to predict which scenario will happen. Choosing two or three isn't about being right. It's about making sure you aren't surprised and frozen. Keep the number small, though. Ten scenarios become a spreadsheet nobody reads. And remember to review them every quarter, because the plausible futures change as the world does.

title: Telling Seasons From Growth
script: Think about a shop that sells winter coats. Every October, sales go up. Every March, they drop. That's not growth, and it's not a problem. It's seasonality: a pattern that repeats at regular times, usually every year. Why does it matter for forecasting? Because if you don't separate the seasonal pattern from real growth, you'll misread the numbers. Say the shop sold twice as many coats in November as in August. A careless planner might say, demand doubled! But a careful one says, it's November. The right comparison is November this year with November last year. If this November is ten percent higher than last November, that's growth. Think of baking bread: in a hot kitchen, the dough rises faster. You don't conclude that your flour got better. You account for the temperature. In the same way, we account for the season. Practically, we do this by estimating a seasonal index for each month, a number showing how far above or below the average that month usually is. We divide the sales by that index to see the underlying trend. Then we forecast the trend and put the seasonal pattern back on top. So we have three pieces to work with: the trend, the seasonal pattern, and random noise.

title: Shipments Are Not Demand
script: Here's a number every planner has: last month's shipments. And here's a mistake almost every new planner makes: treating it as last month's demand. Demand is what customers wanted to buy. Shipments are what we managed to deliver. When there is plenty of stock, the two are the same. But when stock is short, they separate. Say customers ordered a hundred and twenty units, and we only had ninety. We shipped ninety. If the system records ninety as demand, we have just taught the forecast that demand was lower than it really was. Next month, the forecast is lower, we order less, and we run short again. It's a quiet little loop that makes the problem worse each time. People often think shipment history is the safest data because it's the most solid. But it only tells you what was possible, not what was wanted. A better source is the order history: what customers asked for, and when they wanted it. Add the orders that were cancelled because we couldn't deliver, if you have them. If the data isn't there, you can sometimes estimate the lost sales from stockout dates and patterns in the surrounding weeks. Either way, mark the periods when stock was short. Then the next planner will know that those months say less about customers than about the warehouse.

title: The Power of a Pause
script: You make an offer. The other person says nothing. Three seconds pass, then five. It feels like an hour. What do most people do? They fill the gap. They say, well, we could be flexible, or maybe a little lower. And just like that, they've bargained against themselves. The pause is one of the cheapest and most powerful tools in negotiation. After you state your price or your terms, stop talking. Let the other side think. They may be doing arithmetic, checking with someone, or simply deciding how to answer. Either way, the pressure to speak belongs to them. Now, a quick digression: I once read that in some countries a pause in conversation is considered polite, while in others it signals trouble. Anyway, back to the point. Suppose you're buying a machine and the seller asks for forty thousand. You say, that's higher than we planned, and then you wait. Quite often the seller adds, I suppose we could look at thirty-six. You did nothing but stay quiet. Of course, the silence should look calm, not hostile. Keep your posture relaxed, maintain eye contact if it's natural, and count slowly to yourself if you need to. Practice it first in low-stakes situations. It feels unnatural at first, but it gets easier. So after your next offer, try to be the second person to speak.

title: The Monthly Planning Rhythm
script: Let's walk through one month of sales and operations planning, because the rhythm matters more than any single meeting. It starts with data. In the first week, the team cleans up last month's actuals, checks the forecast accuracy and updates the inventory position. Nobody makes decisions here. The goal is simply one set of numbers that everybody trusts. Second comes the demand review. Sales and marketing look at the statistical forecast and adjust it with what they know, like a big tender or a product launch. By the end, you have one agreed demand plan. Side note, I once spent twenty minutes in a demand review debating the color of a chart. It was a lovely shade of teal. Anyway, back to the point. Third is the supply review. Now operations and procurement test whether they can actually deliver that demand with the capacity and materials available. If they can't, they list the gaps and the options. Finally, the executive meeting. Leaders don't want every detail. They want the gaps, the choices and a recommendation, and then they decide. After that, the cycle restarts with the next month's data. So think of it as a funnel: each step narrows the problem until a decision is possible. Next, we'll look at what a good supply review pack actually contains.

title: Who Needs to Hear What
script: So, what is a stakeholder map? It's a simple picture of the people who care about your project, or can affect it. You draw two lines, one for power and one for interest. Power means how much a person can help or block you. Interest means how much they care about the result. That gives you four groups. High power and high interest: these are your key players. Work closely with them. High power but low interest: keep them informed, but don't overload them. Low power but high interest: keep them in the loop, because they often become your supporters. And low power, low interest: just watch. Let me give an example. Say you're changing how a warehouse labels its pallets. The warehouse manager is a key player. The finance director has high power, but doesn't care about labels, so a short monthly note is enough. The drivers care a lot, but can't decide anything. Ask for their ideas anyway. Oh, and I should mention that I once spent a whole weekend on a colour-coded version of this chart. Anyway, back to the point. The map is not the goal. The goal is to decide what each person needs to hear, and when. Put it on one page, update it every month, and use it before every meeting.

title: Why People Resist Better Options
script: Imagine you've built a new forecasting template. It's faster, it's more accurate, and it took you three weeks. You show it to the team, and nobody uses it. That's status quo bias, and it's one of the most stubborn habits in any workplace. People tend to prefer the current situation, simply because it's the current situation. The old spreadsheet may be clumsy, but everyone knows where the traps are. A new tool has traps nobody has found yet, so it feels riskier, even when the numbers say otherwise. Let's say the old template takes four hours every Monday, and the new one takes one hour. Saving three hours a week sounds like an easy win. But the team has to learn new buttons, trust new outputs and fix new mistakes. The cost of changing is felt immediately, while the benefit arrives later. Do you really think people weigh those two things fairly? Of course not. We feel the loss of a familiar routine more strongly than a gain of the same size. So what can you do? Don't just announce the change. Run the old and the new version side by side for a month, and let people see the results themselves. Ask what they'd miss about the old way, and fix that first. We'll look at how to run that pilot month in the next section. For now, the take-away is this: when people resist a better option, don't argue, reduce the felt risk of switching.

title: A Status Update People Read
script: Think of the last status email you received. Did you read all of it? Probably not. Most of us scan the first two lines and move on. So write for that reader. Here's the order that works. First, lead with the answer. Don't start with the history. Say, the January launch is on track, or the January launch is at risk. That's what the reader wants to know. Second, give the risk. One or two sentences about what could go wrong and how likely it is. Third, make the ask. What do you need, from whom, and by when? For example, I need approval for a second supplier by Wednesday. If the ask is buried in paragraph four, it will not get done. Now, I once read an update so long that it came with its own table of contents. Where was I? Right, the structure. The reason it works is simple. Senior readers don't have time for a story. They have time for a decision. Everything else, the detail, the data, the long explanation, can go below, for anyone who wants it. So before you hit send, check your first line. If someone read only that, would they know where you stand? If not, rewrite it. You'll save them time, and you'll get answers faster.

title: Money Already Spent Is Gone
script: You are three months into a software project. You've spent two hundred thousand, and it's clear that the tool won't solve the problem it was meant to. Do you stop? Many teams don't. They say: we've already spent so much, we can't walk away now. This is the sunk cost fallacy. The money is gone whatever you do. The only rational question is what the future costs and benefits look like from today. If finishing requires another hundred thousand to produce something worth fifty, stopping is the better decision, even though it feels like wasting the first two hundred. It's a bit like finishing a bad meal because you paid for it. You don't get the money back, and you just feel worse. I once worked with a team that kept funding a warehouse automation pilot for two extra years, mostly because the director had announced it publicly, and no one wanted to be the person to say it wasn't working. By the end it had cost three times the original budget. I find it frustrating, because the people involved were smart, but the emotional pull of past investment was stronger than their analysis. To fight it, review projects regularly with a fresh question: if we were starting today, knowing what we know, would we begin this? If the answer is no, you have your decision.

title: Matching the Beat of Demand
script: Let me start with a restaurant that's open for dinner. Suppose the kitchen has four hours of service and customers order two hundred and forty meals in that time. That works out to one meal per minute on average. That number is what we call takt time: the rhythm at which customers actually buy. It's calculated by dividing the available working time by customer demand. In a factory with seven hours of work time and demand for four hundred twenty units, takt time is one unit per minute. Now, here's where people get confused. Takt time isn't how fast you can work. Your cycle time, the real time one step takes, might be forty seconds, and that sounds great. But if the customer only buys one every sixty seconds, working at forty means building up stock nobody asked for. By the way, my grandmother used to cook her entire Sunday lunch the night before, because she said it was faster. It probably was. Anyway, back to the point. The takt time sets the beat, and you design the process to match it. If your cycle time is longer than takt, you have a capacity problem. If it is much shorter, you have waste. Having defined the beat, we can look at what happens when demand changes in the middle of the month, and takt time has to be recalculated.

title: Find the Bottleneck First
script: Imagine a production line with four machines in a row. The first can make a hundred units an hour, the second eighty, the third forty, and the fourth ninety. How many units does the whole line produce per hour? Forty. The slowest machine sets the pace for everyone. That machine is the constraint, or the bottleneck, and the theory of constraints is built on this simple observation. It gives you a sequence. First, find the constraint. Second, protect it, which means making sure it never waits for material or stands idle during a lunch break. Third, make everything else support it. And only then, fourth, improve the constraint itself, for example by adding capacity. Notice what that implies. If you speed up machine one, you gain nothing. You just pile up stock in front of machine three. I once watched a company spend a fortune on faster packaging equipment, which, funnily enough, I happened to be reading about on the train that morning. Anyway, back to the point. The money was wasted because packaging wasn't the bottleneck. I find this logic genuinely liberating. It tells you that most of your improvement ideas, however clever, don't matter right now, and that one thing does. So before you improve anything, ask which step limits the whole system.

options: All machines in a line should be improved equally
Improvement should focus on the one step that limits output

questions.explanation: The speaker says to find, protect and then improve the constraint.

One hundred units an hour

questions.explanation: The slowest machine sets the pace at forty.

title: The Cheapest Price Is Rarely Cheapest
script: Let's say you're buying a coffee machine for the office. One costs four hundred euros, and another costs nine hundred. Easy choice? Not quite. The cheap one uses expensive capsules, breaks every year and needs a technician. Over five years, it might cost you more than the machine that looked expensive on day one. This is the idea of total cost of ownership: the full cost of something across its whole life, not only the price you pay at the start. In purchasing, it matters a great deal. Take a packaging supplier whose boxes are two cents cheaper. If those boxes arrive with a higher defect rate, you'll pay for extra inspection, rework and customer complaints. If the supplier is far away, there's longer transport time, so you need more safety stock, and that ties up cash. Add up all those items, and the cheap boxes may be the expensive ones. So how do you calculate it? Make a list of every cost across the full lifetime, and ask the supplier for the data you don't have. First, we'll cover the costs you pay before and during the purchase. After that, we'll look at running costs and the cost of ending the relationship. The take-away: when you compare offers, compare lifetimes, not price tags.

title: Trade, Don't Just Give
script: Here's a simple rule for negotiations: never give something for nothing. When the other side asks for a concession, don't just say yes. Say yes, if. Yes, we can deliver a week earlier, if you increase the order by ten percent. Yes, we can extend your payment terms, if you sign for two years. This is called trading, and it's very different from conceding. A concession gives away value and teaches the other side that asking works. A trade gives away value but gets some in return, so the balance holds. Let's take a concrete case. A customer asks us for free shipping on a thousand-euro order. Shipping costs us fifty euros. If we say fine, we lose fifty. If we say we can include shipping if the order is fifteen hundred, we may earn five hundred more in sales. Of course, some people think trading is rude. In my experience, it is the opposite, because both sides understand the exchange. The only people who truly enjoy one-sided concessions are the ones receiving them, which is hardly a surprise. Also, keep the small things small. Don't trade a major point for a minor one. And before the meeting, list what you can offer cheaply but the other side values highly. Those are your currency. I'm convinced that this habit, more than any clever tactic, protects your margins.

questions.explanation: The rule is 'never give something for nothing'.

title: Air, Sea or Road
script: Air, sea or road? It sounds like an easy choice: fast, cheap or in between. But the real choice is a trade-off between three things: cost, speed and reliability. Air is fast, usually a day or two across the world, but it costs many times more per kilo. Sea is cheap, especially for heavy loads, but it can take a month, and delays at ports are common. Road sits in the middle. It's flexible, door to door, and good for short and medium distances, but it depends on drivers, fuel and borders. Let's say you must move a product from Asia to Europe. If the item is small and valuable, and a stockout would cost you a lot, air may be worth it. If it's bulky and you can plan ahead, sea is the sensible choice. By the way, I once met a ship's captain who said he had never seen the sea calm on a Monday. Anyway, back to transport. One more thing: don't pick the mode once and forget it. Many planners ship by sea normally, and keep air as an emergency option. That emergency option must be agreed and budgeted in advance, or it will arrive as a surprise bill. So think of the mode as a tool you choose for each product and each situation, not a fixed habit.

title: Averages Hide the Swings
script: Here's a claim that surprises people: you can run out of stock even when your average demand is lower than your average supply. How is that possible? Because averages hide the swings. Imagine a supermarket checkout. On average, a cashier can serve one customer per minute, and on average one customer arrives per minute. In theory, no queue. But in reality, customers arrive in bunches. Three come at once, then nobody for two minutes. During the bunch, a queue appears, and the people at the back wait much longer than the average suggests. It's the same in supply chains. Suppose a product sells one hundred units a week on average. If one week sells forty and the next one hundred sixty, your average is still one hundred, but you will have an empty shelf in the second week unless you hold stock. The same applies to supplier lead times. A supplier that delivers in ten days on average, but sometimes takes twenty, forces you to plan for twenty. That's why many experienced planners consider variability the real enemy. I find it hard to take any plan seriously when it's built only on the average, because the average never visits the warehouse. Always ask for the spread: the best case, the worst case and how often each happens. Reduce the swings if you can, and protect yourself against them when you can't.

questions.explanation: The speaker says averages hide the swings that cause empty shelves.
